utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may begin, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness says he cannot hear properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a technical problem. Can we have that attended to and corrected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Slobodan Jarcevic. I was born on the 2nd of February, 1942, in Gornje Ravno, Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am one of the babies, few babies that survived of the Croatian Holocaust against the Jews and Serbs in my native region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, something about your education and your professional life.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: My family was from Bosnia. It relocated to Serbia pursuant to a Serbian government decision in 1946 where I went to primary school and secondary school and graduated at the Faculty of Political Sciences in Belgrade. I am a member of the Association of Writers of Serbia. I worked for 33 years. I was a diplomat of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you serve?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I served in Zambia, India, Greece, Romania, and Kuwait for a certain amount of time, whether it be shorter or longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what functions did you have during the war in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: From October 1992 until April 1994, I was minister of foreign affairs of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, and from April 1994 until 1996, I was foreign policy advisor to the president of Srpska Krajina, Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that that is sufficient as regards your CV. We don't need any further details for the time being. To start off with, I'm going to ask you something that you have direct knowledge of and which is connected to the indictment for Croatia. You were therefore, as you said, the foreign minister in Krajina for most of the time. Now, in the Croatia indictment, referring to responsibility and accountability or, rather, paragraph 6, it says that some sort of joint criminal enterprise existed, the purpose of which was the forcible removal of the majority of the Croat and other non-Serb population from the territory of the Republic of Croatia, that I allegedly planned to become part of a new Serb-dominated state.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: That kind of plan is an illusion. It never existed. In Belgrade there was no politician there in Serbia or Montenegro. A criminal enterprise just existed in the top political parties of Croatia, their top echelons, and in the authorities of Croatia. It had as its purpose to do away from the Croatia that was formed in AVNOJ and AVNOJ [as interpreted] all the Serbs, and to do so in one way or another. There are many facts about that, including United Nations documents which testify to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it mean to do away with all Serbs in one way or another? In what way to dispose of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: For us to be able to understand that, we have to understand the doctrine of the Croatian state. From the 19th century its programme was as follows: Croatia, without any Orthodox Serbs in it. They must either be destroyed, expelled, or Croatised, having converted them to Catholicism before that. And I think that it is very interesting for the Trial Chamber to hear from me that this was done through school textbooks. In each of the school textbooks, it says that the father of the Croatian state is Ante Starcevic, and he wrote in the 19th century that Serbs were citizens of a lower order and that they should be beaten with an axe. So for 60 years, in all the school textbooks and university textbooks, that formulation survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but let's go back to the material period that is incorporated in the indictment. Tell us this, please: When did violence and crimes in that area begin and who perpetrated them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: When I said that Croatia had as its doctrine the annihilation of the Serbs, if we -- if we don't take into account what the Austrians did to the Croats in World War I, the second attempt to persecute the Serbs and expulse them from present-day Croatia began in 1939 under the direct demands of the fascist countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, Mr. Milosevic, to his credit, directed you to speak about the time covered by the indictment, but you have gone back to the 1930s and 1940s. Just concentrate on the question asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have completed what I wanted to say about 1939. The next attempt at Serb expulsion was in 1971, and persecution, with the so-called maspok, or mass movement in Croatia, which was not a long time ago, and it was the cadres which led this Croatian spring, or maspok, with the intention of persecuting the Serbs were at the beginning of the political parties in 1990. And among them we have Franjo Tudjman, Stipe Mesic, Djapic, and the rest of the leaders of today's political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's stick to that time frame and those years. Tell us what your knowledge is about what actually the Croatian authorities had been planning for the territory inhabited by Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It is probably very difficult for those of you who do not come from the Balkans to understand all the religious and nationalistic complications of the former Yugoslavia, but when it comes to Croatia, we'll be able to show this best taking the example of the European countries. Croatia was the same thing that Belgium is today. That is to say a bi-national state, a state of the Croats and the Serbs. The first things the Croatian leaders planned to do is this: They planned to have this bi-national or two-nation Croatia turned into a one-nation Croatia, and not to call it the state of the Serbs and Croats any more but just the state of the Croats. That was the lever which would trigger off all the terrible events that came to pass later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the political situation in Croatia in 1990?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It was a terrible situation, precisely because the constitution had been changed, and that two-nation state was turned into a single-nation state, and measures immediately followed that were very stringent towards the Serbs, brutal towards the Serbs. They started throwing Serbs out of their jobs, first all out of the police stations, then the explanation they had given for dismissing Serbs was the kind that was never noted in any country anywhere in the world. For example, a certain man is being dismissed from his job because he is not showing sufficient respect for the Croatian authorities. That was one of the formulations that you would find in letters of dismissal to thousands and thousands of Serbs from Dubrovnik, Split, Zadar, Karlovac, Rijeka, all these people being dismissed. And they were living far away from the subject matter this Trial Chamber is involved in Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are talking about areas in Croatia that are not incorporated in the definition of the territory of Srpska Krajina's autonomous provinces and so on, districts and so on and so forth, the SAOs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm very surprised to see that there wasn't an indictment raised by the Prosecution against those who expelled 400.000 Serbs from Croatian towns. That is the largest ethnic cleansing on the territory of the former Yugoslavia that ever took place. And there are documents to bear this out from the Security Council, and I can say a few words about them if the Trial Chamber would be interested in hearing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said a few words about the general climate that prevailed and the events that took place in 1990. Now, how did the Serbs react in Croatia to those events and to those developments and that general mood that prevailed, the violence that threatened them and that happened to them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: In 1990, or the year 1990 froze the marrow in the Serb bones, as we like to say. There are probably similar proverbs in other languages too. Let me tell you, in 1990 the Serb leader Raskovic, in Sibenik and Zadar, was shown a petition with signatures saying that he should move out of town, and one of the foremost journalists of Croatia, Tanja Torbarina, in 1990, in the paper Vjesnik says, "I'm not a racist. Who can say that I am just for the fact that I hate Serbs more than I hate blacks?" What does that mean? It means what she considers the Serbs -- the blacks to be a low race and the blacks an even lower race -- and the Serbs an even lower race. I have one of those articles here. It says the Serbs are livestock from the east. You can never teach them anything, and they behave like a bull in a china shop. Along with articles of this kind, and even worse articles, you had Serb houses being set fire to and destroyed, as well as shops, et cetera, and this was still far away from the Republic of Srpska Krajina. There were Sisak, Zagreb, and Dubrovnik where this was going on. For example, Dubrovnik is being mentioned here quite a lot and he experienced 2.200 Serbs being expelled. If you take it that a family has three family members, that is 700 households that were looted, seized and so on. Seven hundred houses were seized, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the Serbs froze in their bones, was that a general fear or can you pinpoint that fear to individual geographic areas in Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the threats came through the mass media, and if they weren't direct threats, then there was news passed by the media saying one house had just been set on fire, or another economic facility, another shop, and you would always hear the name and surname of the owner, which means that you could recognise through these names that they were Serb names and Serbs who were under jeopardy, nobody else. Just some Serbs happened to be protected if there were some reasonable men at a local level that didn't look -- listen to what they were being ordered either by the police or from state institutions. However, it is difficult today to recognise which those areas in fact were, because there is no single region of Croatia, I say further afield from the Republic of Srpska Krajina, whose inhabitants do not live as fugitives all over the world; in the United States of America, Australia, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did the different political parties in Croatia begin to appear, and what was the attitude taken by the main political parties in Croatia with respect to current policy and the security policy and situation in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that the HDZ and the Croatian Rights Movement -- Party, and perhaps some others that directly relied upon the ideology of Ante Starcevic to the effect that the Serbs should be beaten with an axe, other parties too had similar party programmes against the Serbs but they did not publicly manifest them. I cannot see that there was a single party in Croatia with a programme to protect the Serbs and to preserve Croatia as a two-nation state. There was nobody in the Sabor or parliament voting against any changes in the constitution which would enact a single-nation state instead of a two-nation state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to the Serb political -- Serb political organisation at that time, that is to say when those events took place and when they unfolded? So what was the behaviour and conduct of the Serbian Democratic Party, for example?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The political activity of the Serbs at that time was supra-national, supra-ethnic, and the Serbs joined parties which also had Croats among their members. They hoped that through the policy of Yugoslavia that had been implemented up to that time, the policy of brotherhood and unity that had been in force since World War II, they would preserve Yugoslavia and suppress this dangerous Croatian nationalism as had been done in 1971. However, they soon realised that the Croatian cadres in these common or joint political parties were not contributing to the implementation of this policy. Croatian voters mostly voted for parties which openly expressed their programme and their wish to have Croatia become a one-nation state. The plan was in 1990 to make Croatia a state devoid of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who were the main organisers of this policy in Croatia all this time? Not in history. I am not asking you about history now but about that time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Franjo Tudjman was at the top of it all, because -- I do have to go a little way back into the past. There were Croatian emigres in many Western countries - Australia, America, England, France - and they gave him selfless assistance in money and everything else, and propaganda. The president of Croatia today, Mesic, Racan, and everybody had the same kind of policy. No one can deny that all the leaders of all the Croatian political parties were preparing for what was to happen in 1991 and 1992. That is the expulsion of Serbs from Croatian towns. It might be interesting to explain why the towns were the first: Because the Krajina was sparsely populated, and in the former Yugoslavia it had been neglected. There was no industrial development. Industrial development took place in towns. This naturally moved the Serbs from the Krajina to go to the cities on the coast where there was tourism, or to Zagreb, which was a large industrial centre, to Karlovac, Rijeka, Osijek, and so on. The majority of the Serb population was no longer in the Krajina. According to the information received from the Croatian embassy in New York, there were 471.000 Serbs in the towns, whereas there were only 251.000 in the Krajina. If we add those figures up, we see to what extent the Croatian state was indoctrinated against the Serbs. Official statistical data said that there was only 581.000 Serbs in Croatia; however, if you add up these two figures, you see it's over 700.000. In Knin in 1992 and 1993, we re-checked these figures, and it appears that there were over a million Serbs in Croatia. One could reconstruct this taking into account the Croatian information from the Security Council mentioning 471.000 Serbs. Why? Because these were the Serbs in all the municipalities added up, and this is more convincing than the census that was published at republican level. Evidently the number of Serbs was always reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was fear among the Serbs because of all these events that you have mentioned. Was there anything coming from Belgrade that might fan the flames of that fear?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, for heaven's sake, was there any impulse needed from outside the borders of Croatia to lead the Serbs to conclude they were in mortal danger? The same kind of measures taken by Franjo Tudjman's government had been literally implemented in 1941 in fascist Croatia. One doesn't have to be highly intelligent to realise that the Croatian authorities were to take up arms and take the same road they had taken in 1941. Had there been a Great Wall of China between Serbia and Montenegro and the Croatia of today, the Serbs would probably have been even more determined to defend themselves. This way, they placed their hopes in the Yugoslav People's Army, and they perhaps prepared to a lesser extent than they should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did this violence in Croatia begin specifically?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It began in 1990 when Croatian newspapers were full of the kind of writing I've just described. And all the Serbs who were employed in the police, that is the Ministry of the Interior, were dismissed from their jobs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, are you reading from notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have to read, but I can if you like, because I have brought some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I just need to know whether you're reading from notes and, if you are, then whether you have prepared the notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was about to come here, a man downloaded from the internet something that the Serbian forum in Zagreb had posted on the internet, and it is some information which is hard to memorise, although in 1992 and 1993, when I was minister, I knew it all by heart, but you can't expect a man to remember every detail. However, I will speak in general. And you can get all this information from the Croatian government, which I think is duty-bound, as is the Yugoslav government, to provide information to this Tribunal. In 1990, dismissals of policemen began. According to the information gathered by the Serb Democratic Forum, headed by Pupovac, you can see that dozens of policemen were dismissed in every town. People who were dismissed from their jobs in various companies or government jobs, that is not recorded anywhere, but you can compare this to the statistical data in Serbia and Montenegro where these people arrived as refugees. Of course, in 1992, the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina asked all the countries to which these people had gone in Western Europe, Canada, America, Australia, to give us this information and to tell us how many Serbs had arrived in these countries in 1993 who had left Croatian towns, but no government gave us this information. We sent several notes to the Security Council, asking them to ask their members and the members of the UN to get this information from their immigration authorities, but they refused to give us this data. However, let me add something that's very interesting. Boutros-Ghali, when we exerted pressure on him, on the 15th of May, 1993, read out that the number of Serbs who had fled to the Krajina and to Serbia and Montenegro amounted to 251.000. If one trusts the Secretary-General, then the information provided by the Croatian embassy about 471.000 Serbs is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, in connection with the figures are you mentioning, you have brought here a copy of a letter from the then Croatian ambassador containing some of this information. It's in tab 16. Can you please look at it and tell us about this information.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have to look at it. I think I know it off by heart. The Croatian embassy is informing the Security Council that in the Krajina, that is in the UN protected area, there are only 189.000 Croats. However, if we look at the extent of the suffering -- that's not it. If we look at the extent of the suffering of the Serbs and Croats, when you look at the number of Serbs who were there and the number of Croats who were on the other side, you will see that there were two and a half times more Serbs who suffered than the number of Croats who were withdrawn in an organised manner from the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you pause for a moment, please. You've just said "withdrawn in an organised manner" referring to Serbs from the territory of the Republic of Srpska Krajina. What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we use basic logic, the fact that in the world -- the fact that 471.000 Serbs were expelled has been concealed. One wonders how the media and the UN could have overlooked this. Then of course it was much easier on the Croatian side to organise the departure of the Serbs from the Serbian Krajina, and there were only 189.000 of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who organised the departure from the Republic of Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: As I said, it was organised by the Croatian government in order to demonstrate to the world how cruel the Serbs were and how they could not tolerate people of other ethnicities or religions. This kind of language was omnipresent and can be found even in the most prestigious European and American media. Of the 471.000 Serbs that I've mentioned, there is no information to this very day that this was ever discussed in any UN body, for example, or any body of the European Union, or anywhere else except - and we may come to this - that the Republic of Serbian Krajina received some signals from European international organisations to the effect that this is an issue that will soon be raised. And it's already been raised at the session of the Council of Europe of the 26th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have directed our attention to tab 16, the letter from the Croatian ambassador to the Secretary-General of the UN. There's an explanatory memorandum. What part of the memorandum do you wish us to attend to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't finished with this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just let me have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I'm asking Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page, Mr. Nort.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this explanatory memorandum that he has provided, figures are mentioned. I was only interested in the figures that Mr. Jarcevic could comment upon. As to the political explanations, these are irrelevant for our purposes. These are political phrases used at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The second paragraph. What is the point of directing us to a memorandum and you don't tell us what aspect of it you wish to rely on? In the second paragraph there is a reference to some figures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the second paragraph there are some figures mentioned. You see, it says here as a result --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look, Mr. Jarcevic, at paragraph 2, and I will ask you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: What tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sixteen. This is the letter dated the 27th of May, 1994, sent by the permanent mission of the Republic of Croatia to the United Nations. It's a letter signed by Mario Nobilo, and there are figures that are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for them to assist me. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I -- have you found it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. The gentleman helped me, and I'm grateful to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you whether these figures that the Croatian government is submitting to the Secretary-General are correct. It says here: "According to the census of 1991, [In English] 500.000 -- 533.202 people lived in territories that are presently under Serbian occupation." [Interpretation] Were these territories under Serbian occupation at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Look here: The Croats say here that there are 533.000 people who lived there. Of them, 271.000 were Serbs, and there were 72.000 others. These were Yugoslavs, but 80 per cent of those were Serbs again. So if we were to add this up, there were 320.000 Serbs. And as the Croatian ambassador says, there were 189.000 Croats. It's really impossible that the Serbs occupied their own country. This has entered the political vocabulary of the world, and it is a wonder that this has survived to this day. Secondly, the Croats say that the Serbs expelled 251.000 Croats from the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where does he say that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I think it's in the very next letter, if you -- here it is: 250.000 Croats were expelled from the occupied parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where do we find that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tab 17?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must manage your case better than you're doing. We are now being asked to look at tab 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, about six lines up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where it says, under point 3, in the middle of that paragraph: "[In English] About 250.000 Croats have been expelled from the occupied areas of Croatia." [Interpretation] So more Croats were expelled than had lived there, according to the census?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 60.000 more, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, as you were the minister of foreign affairs of the Krajina, were there any Croats in those areas during the war; in Knin, in other towns? Were there any Croats there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, I can't give you the numbers because I didn't delve into that at the time, but there were Croats in Knin, Vukovar, Baranja, and several villages in Lika. However, one should know that many Croats were employed in the administration of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, and some even joined the army. A few days ago, I ran into a man, a Croat, who until 2005 had been the commander of the garrison in Mladenovci, which is 60 kilometres south of Belgrade. He retired only last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To sum up, what, according to you, are the realistic figures demonstrating how many Serbs lived in Croatia, how many were expelled, and where they went?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are no realistic figures to be found anywhere today. Unfortunately, in the former Yugoslavia in many republics and provinces, when the census was taken, the results were forged. For example, in Kosovo, a far larger number of Siptars was shown to be there and a far smaller number of Serbs. In 1993 in Knin, the government tried to get more precise information about the Serbs in the former Croatia, and they arrived at a number which was over a million. In Croatia there were between 22 and 25 per cent Serbs and not 12 per cent, as Croatian statistics falsely represented. I wish to draw attention once again to the number the Croats obtained by adding up the numbers of Serbs in the various municipalities, which they handed over to the Secretary-General. There were 471.000 Serbs in the big towns alone. Unfortunately, this document was seized by the Croatian police as was the entire archives in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not dwell on this any longer and let's move on. To the best of your knowledge, how many Serbs fled from Croatia in 1990 and 1991? I'm not talking about what happened later, the attacks that took place during Flash and Storm and Western Slavonia, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I am not competent to utter that figure in my own name on the basis of the information that the government of the Krajina had. As I said, these documents were seized. But let us rely on Boutros-Ghali's report that says that until the beginning of 1993, that is to say in 1991, 1992 and 1993, the following number was expelled only to Yugoslavia and to Krajina, that is 251.000 Serbs. Only Germany reacted to our letter when in 1993 we asked European countries to give us information about the number of Serbs who sought shelter there. However, the reaction of the German state was very strange. They only said that all of those who came to Croatia -- to Germany from Croatia would be returned. Of course, that led the government of the Serb Krajina to write a note to the German embassy in Belgrade and ask them to tell the government not to return people to areas where they were in danger. That is a very basic tenet of the UN: You cannot return refugees to areas where they would live under the threat of robbery, killing, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to endeavour to answer more briefly. Concentrate on the question. There is a tendency to digress. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said now, in view of these documents of the United Nations, that the representatives of the international community knew about the magnitude of the problem that existed then and they knew about this great wave of refugees, Serb refugees from those areas outside the Republic of Serb Krajina, the Serb refugees that fled from other parts of Croatia. Did you personally talk to any representatives of the international community about that, in view of the fact that you were foreign minister?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with many, but I'm afraid that the Chamber is going to say that I go on and on at great length. However, if noteworthy, I'm going to describe these conversations. Gert Ahrends --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Gert Ahrends.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I remember him, yes, Ambassador Gert Ahrends. He spoke Serbian.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: He spoke Serbian better than I do. Then Kofi Annan as well, then General Wahlgren, then I talked to Cyrus Vance about this in February 1993. If you find this of interest, I can tell you about what was said during these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us just as briefly as possible. What did you talk about to Gert Ahrends?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: As for Gert Ahrends, I talked to him about refugees from Croat towns in Germany, and he said the German government is not going to give you any information in writing, and the embassy in Belgrade is not going to give any information; however, what I am conveying to you is that the German government gave up on returning Serb ex-police from Croatian towns. They will remain in Germany, although Germany has the largest expenses among all the European countries in terms of supporting such refugees. And then he went on to other matter that are not that interesting. Then I talked to Cyrus Vance about all of this. Our delegation was in New York then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: February 1993. That was before the Secretary-General read that 251.000 Serbs were expelled from Croat towns to Yugoslavia and to the Republic of Serb Krajina. And then when I talked to Vance, I was on the delegation that was led by Goran Hadzic, the president of the Republic of Serb Krajina. I took the floor, and we and the Croats and Vance had the draft Resolution 815 in our hands then. I asked Mr. Vance the following: If this draft Resolution is ultimately adopted, then your own plan, the Vance Plan, will go down the drain, because the Resolution will say that the Republic of Serb Krajina is part of Croatia, the Republic of Croatia. Mr. Vance, are you not going to protect your own plan? You have time to intervene with the Security Council. He kept silent for a long time, and then he said the Security Council has too great an authority for me to be able to intervene. Then I asked both him and Thornberry, who sat next to him, why there is no mention in these resolutions of the persecution of Serbs and their expulsion from Croat towns. Why is there no mention of that? Why is there no punishment for that? He kept quiet and he said that nothing could be done against Croatia because no Resolution envisages any such thing. That is to say that no Resolution calls for Croatia to do that. That was quite a surprise. I could not believe it, why no one had to be punished if they persecuted Serbs or expelled Serbs. I asked him about another matter, too. If you think, Mr. President, I can talk about that as well, but can I tell you about Kofi Annan's reaction?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Kofi Annan at that time was under-secretary for operations, and these operations were taking place in the UNPAs; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: He was commander of the peace forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was no commander of the peace forces. He was the under-secretary in charge of peace operations of the UN throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what he was. He visited Knin. He had a meeting with the government, and the deputy Prime Minister spoke, Branko Lubovac, and he asked Mr. Kofi Annan, "What about the officers and soldiers who are in the Serb Krajina? Are they not going to protect the Serbs?" He expressed his doubts. He thought that they would not do that because he mentioned this expulsion of Serbs from Croat towns. However, Kofi Annan got visibly angry - he even raised his voice - and he said, "Officers and soldiers who serve here on -- within the peacekeeping missions will keep their military honour, and they will protect your people." After that meeting, I asked him, "Mr. Kofi Annan, this republic of ours of the Serb Krajina, which is officially called a UNPA, why is it now under UN sanctions? Is there any logic involved there that you who are protecting us are now punishing us so severely, which is going to lead to the population that sought refuge from the Croat towns leave?" I was surprised. Mr. Kofi Annan hugged me. He put his arms around me, and he said, "Let's go and have lunch. We really made a mistake. We don't know how to get out of all this." And then also I talked to General Wahlgren on the plane when we went to Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. General Wahlgren was for awhile commander of the UN peace forces.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a Norwegian, and in March we were on the same plane, travelling to Geneva where, after the New York negotiations, the same talks continued in Geneva. Then I asked Mr. Wahlgren why no document of the UN mentions the Serbs who were expelled from towns. And he said no, no, no, that is referred to. And he called one of his officers on the plane and he said give me all the documents, give me all the Resolutions of the Security Council. And they were reading all of this as we were flying over Croatia, Austria, all the way to Geneva. And then he said, "Mr. Jarcevic, indeed there is no mention, but I'm going to do my best that this is referred to." And he promised that he would raise the question in New York of the expulsion of Serbs from Croatian towns. However, I think this was sometime in August 1993, and he was transferred from the peace forces there. And I said, "Mr. Wahlgren, what happened?" And he said, "Mr. Boutros Boutros-Ghali did that to me in his democratic circle," the democratic circle around him, under quotation marks. So that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to the first commander of the UN Protection Force, the Indian general, Nambiar, General Nambiar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a very interesting conversation at the beginning of 1993. I was minister for only three months then and he was about to leave, and I paid him a farewell call and I asked him, "General, tell me, why is there no mention of the expelled Serbs from Croatian towns?" He was visibly moved. He went silent. He put his head down, and I hope that you will believe me because I do not have any documents corroborating this. That was also seized in Knin. He said: "Well, there is mention of that. The Security Council has detailed information about crimes committed against Serbs in Croatia and detailed information about the expulsion of Serbs that you are asking me about now, but believe me, Minister -" he even called me a minister - "this information is in the Security Council, but they are sealed off." This is a terrible thing to say, I know, but I swore to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Parallel to what happened at the beginning of the conflict and the initial tensions in Croatia, do you know until when Serb representatives were involved in regular political life and were -- how long were they in the Croatian parliament too?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, at that time I was not a member of the Krajina government. I already said I came in mid-October 1992 when this had already happened. But it so happens that I know three persons from the then Croatian parliament in 1992. That's Marko Atlagic, who has already testified here; Mr. Ratko Licina; and -- how can I not remember the third name? Maybe I'll remember. Yes, Rade Tanga. He was a member of parliament who was seen by the entire world because he went up to the rostrum and he spoke about the bi-national Croatia, and he wanted to say something about the statehood of the Serb peoples sending back to the days of Austria. And he uttered a sentence, and he said that that statehood supersedes the statehood of the Croatian people. And then one of the MPs threw his briefcase at him and walked up to him, threatening him physically. So that is how Serb MPs fared in the Croatian parliament. What I have here is the Serb constitution from 1630. If you wish, I can show it on this overhead projector and you will see that Serbs in Austria had their municipal courts, had their Supreme Court, and no organisation or no court from Austria had the right to intervene except for the emperor himself. When Mr. Tanga wanted to say that, and when he wanted to call the Croatian MPs to reason, not turning Croatia into a one-nation state, I told you how he fared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you follow what happened and what led to the referendum on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serb people in Croatia? When did this referendum take place? What was the reason for it to be held, and how did this happen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, when you asked me whether anybody organised the persecution of Croats, of course there was no mention of that, not in a single Serb party or a Serb body or a Serb organisation. The Serbs, as always, wanted Yugoslavia to be preserved. And then, when they saw that the Croatian MPs started voting the way they did, as I've already explained, then they tried, in that State of Croatia, to win at least cultural autonomy, because they realised that the Croats would not say that there were two equal peoples, peoples who had statehood within Croatia, that there would be no going back to that. When this persecution of Serbs started and when more and more were being expelled from the cities, and when they realised that this was no joking matter at all, I cannot remember the exact dates of all of this, but then they moved on and held a referendum. 99 per cent of the population, I think, of the Republic of Serb Krajina voted in favour of creating a state of their own, as the Serbs presented in 1945. I don't want to be criticised for going back to the past all the time, but I would like to draw your attention to a paper that was part of obtaining a master's degree at the University of Belgrade, and this has to do with Serb-Croatian relations. And then at their Congress in 1945, on the 29th and 30th of September - and this Congress was held in Zagreb, no less - they voted in favour of a resolution asking that the future Yugoslavia cannot cut off ties with all the Serbs within it, including Serbs living in Croatia. So this will and content of the resolution of the Serb people dating back to 1945 was denied. And may I repeat that they were the only protagonists of the anti-fascist struggle in Croatia during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the MA thesis, but you just take that as a source. The document exists, doesn't it, what you mentioned? And you were talking about the resolution of the Serb Congress at the end of the World War II.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it was held in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have a book about it. I can read out the sentence, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just read that one sentence out.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I have to get it out of my bag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do we really need that? He has already spoken about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Robinson, not that. It would be interesting for us to hear it regardless of whether you're going to consider it or not. He's mentioning a master's degree paper as the source of a document because he didn't find it anywhere else, but the document is a well-known one. It exists. So perhaps he could be allowed to read just one sentence out, if that is possible. If not, we can, of course, move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll allow him to read one sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it will take me some time to find the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Never mind. We'll read it after the break. You can find it during the break and, not to lose time, we can read it afterwards. Let's move on now. In connection with the referendum that you spoke about just now, tell us, but just briefly, please, whether the authorities from Belgrade, the Republic of Serbia, took part in the organisation of that referendum or in any way influenced the outcome of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The authorities could not influence the outcome of the referendum. I don't say that there were not people from Serbia who went to assist and offer advice over there and to give guidelines, organisationally speaking, to their relations, because - perhaps the Chamber knows this or not - in Serbia there are 2 million Serbs who originated from Krajina and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they still have their houses and land, both in Krajina and in Bosnia. So of course they went to stay with their relations and help them out. Now, as far as the authorities are concerned, they had no influence whatsoever on the events, because the Serbs in Krajina had organised themselves to defend their very life and their property as well. And for that you don't need any incentive from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in Krajina at the time, were there a number of parties? When I say numerous parties, I mean parties the membership of which was largely made up of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, there were a number of parties, and mostly they were made up of Serb members. However, they did not have the same programmes. For example, Mikelic's party had a pro-Yugoslav programme. Then there was another party, I don't know its exact title, but it was a social democratic party and it too had a Yugoslav programme. And that was the best sign that the Serbs were not as extreme nationalists as the Croats were in their political parties. But when we saw that the Croats were not ready to lend a helping hand to Yugoslavia or to a two-nation Croatia, then all these people turned towards the Serbian Radical Party -- or, rather, the Serbian Democratic Party. That was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Towards the SDS, which was the ruling party.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You also had the Serb Radical Party over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And which party were you a member of? You were a minister in the government of Krajina yourself. Which party did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia until 1990, and from 1990 onwards, throughout the time of my political activity in the Republic of Serbian Krajina I was not a member of any single party, and I informed the government that I would not join up either with the Serbian Democratic Party -- that I would not join the Serbian Democratic Party either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the political, league -- well, I'm not going to ask you about that. We've heard that from other witnesses, all the changes that took place in laws and so on. I'll skip over all that, because you were talking about political and legal changes in Croatia in 1990 and 1991. Now, what happened on the ground? Do you remember any specific event or events which followed those political and legal changes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've already talked about this in one of your first questions. There was dismissal from work. There was dismissal from the police stations and the Ministry of the Interior, of Serbs; the pilfering and looting of houses, setting fire to houses, destroying houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you've already spoken about all this, these phenomena. Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I have a court ruling from Zadar dating back to one month where a Serb lady - I have it in my bag - a Serb lady is being accorded damages because her house was looted three times in 1990, and then damaged and destroyed and razed to the ground. So I have the document in my briefcase. And I assume your associates have that document too. I gave it to them, I think a month ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll take a look at what it says in the document, but --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, Mr. President, but in one of the tabs, a report of the Secretariat of the Interior of Zadar, that is to say Croatia, you have the number of explosions. Perhaps we could see it on the overhead projector, the gentleman could perhaps place it on the overhead projector, because it is a Croatian source, a Croatian police source. So you can see that there were hundreds of explosions and fires planted just in the town of Zadar itself. And Zadar is small coastal town on the Adriatic coast, and it 28.000 Serbs living in it. Of course, all of them, every single one of them were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, from Zadar and the surrounding parts Serbs were expelled. We've heard about that. Did they, the Serbs in Zadar, ever give rise to this behaviour towards them, cause it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't give any cause for such brutal behaviour there or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Osijek and other towns in which no Serb forms of organisation and defence were set up?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: In all Croatian towns where there was no Serb organisation or membership in the Serb Democratic Party, pogroms came to pass. And let me tell you that a few days ago I saw documents from Sisak whereby lawyers from Zagreb - and I'd like to thank them - the lawyers from Zagreb sent in to this Tribunal a piece of evidence about 600 Serbs killed in Sisak and the surrounding parts. The same thing happened in Osijek, the Drava River area, where there were bodies in 1990. And in Osijek a very good local leader, he was a German by origin, wanted to prevent this onslaught by the Croatian police and soldiers against Serb civilians, but he was, unfortunately, killed. I'm very sorry about that, I can't remember his name, but the first refugees into Serbia were from Vukovar. Perhaps you have an erroneous opinion of that town. Vukovar and the surrounding parts had a Serb majority population. Let's go back to before World War II, a much greater majority. And the rest of the Vukovar inhabitants were Germans and Roma. In the Independent State of Croatia during World War II, not a single Roma --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, who carried out these expulsions? How were they carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's so easy. So simple. It was done by the Croatian state. All the organs of the Croatian state persecuted the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but give me the state officials. What state officials carried out these expulsions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was lucky enough not to have been living in Croatia at the time so I can't tell you the name of the man who expelled people from a certain town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, the organs, I see. The head of state, Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was at the head and led everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to find out who carried out the expulsions. Was it the police or the army or what body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The expulsions? Well, simple again, Mr. President. It's very simple: The Croatian state armed almost all adult Croatian males. They set up the Zengas, the ZNGs. They were a paramilitary formation. So they were the ones that did it. The police didn't stop them, they helped them. They helped them hide or keep the identity of the perpetrators hidden. For example, there were 28.000 Serbs expelled from Zadar, and just imagine if from -- 28.000 Croats had been expelled from a Serb town, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who carried out the looting of Serb houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The looting was carried out by -- I apologise for interrupting you. The question is a simple one: The looting was carried out by the paramilitaries and the next-door neighbours, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago, Mr. Jarcevic -- you asked what would have happened had 28.000 Croats been expelled from Serbia, for instance. What would have happened if only 28 Croats were expelled from Serbia? Have you ever heard of even 28 Croats being expelled from Serbia, or two Croats, for that matter, or any Croat being expelled from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And have you ever heard of any Croat being killed in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: No. Today, Mr. President, there are more Croats in Serbia - I happened to read some statistical data a few days ago - than there were in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you speak about the protagonists of those expulsions and persecutions, do you remember the public statements made by Tudjman and Mesic as a function of those expulsions and persecutions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. President. I think it was in 1991 when Stipe threatened that the Croatian state, once it is established, will enable all the Serbs in Croatia to fit under a single umbrella.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think you've mixed the dates up rather. Mesic spoke about that in 1990 in Gospic, in the pre-election campaign, pre-election speech. It's a famous speech of his when he said that all the Serbs would fit under a single umbrella once the state is formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now Mr. Milosevic is actually giving the evidence. The witness does obviously not know about the event enough that he can even place it in location and time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Refrain from giving evidence. Let the witness give the evidence, if he can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was just adding an explanation to what he knows and to what everybody knows in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is not the time for explanations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, did you personally talk to people at that time who were leaving Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I talked to many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those who were fleeing from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was terrible to listen to all the stories of these families. For example, Boro Kutic was a policeman in Pakrac, and he says that just one local paper published the fact that he sent weapons to Knin for the log revolution. At that point in time, nobody wanted to talk to his children in school. I mean the Croatian children didn't want to talk to his children, and his senior called him and said that he should resign and leave his job. What could be worse? Or, for example, in Zagreb - this is quite unbelievable - people were incited to convert to Catholicism, saying that nothing would happen to them if they did so. In the government we had three documents about this, and we asked the Security Council and the Vatican, His Holiness Pope John Paul II, to treat these cases in the way that the Human Rights Charter demands under point E, I think, the crime of genocide. However, nobody turned a -- everybody turned a blind eye to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jarcevic. Mr. Milosevic -- Mr. Milosevic, would you just explain to me what your case is as to how these acts against the Serbs relate to the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are related in such a way, Mr. Robinson, that we can look at the events and see that the Serbs in Croatia exclusively defended themselves, and that the war was the product of the armed secession and a highly brutal form of violence towards them and that, faced with a situation of that kind, they had to organise themselves, and that certainly once there was a clash, there were clashes and conflicts, there were crimes too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you able to direct me to any paragraph in the indictment, to any particular allegation in relation to which any of the evidence given by Mr. Jarcevic points to a response by the Serbs, or are we just at large and speaking in general terms?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not at large and in general terms. I quoted at the beginning a part of the indictment according to which there was a plan to expel the Croats --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the fact that this was the territory where the Serbs lived and where many who were expelled from the rest of Croatia had taken refuge, and that all that was a form of their defence and their protection and the realisation of their right to self-defence. And ultimately you saw that the Vance Plan defined UNPA zones, and we quoted what it says in the plan, to protect the population in those areas, that is to say to protect the Serb population. Why would somebody have to protect themselves if they were not under threat? So the United Nations protected them then. And since they didn't protect them as they had promised to do, so they endeavoured to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But after the arrival of the United Nations, there was not a single aggressive act against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. In my view, it would be to the better if you could relate his evidence more specifically to the charges in the indictment. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the Serbs were converted to Catholicism. What happened to the Serb Orthodox church in Croatia at that time? How was it possible that there was this process to convert them, because there was the Serb Orthodox Church there. It existed and had existed previously. So what happened to the church, the Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It was terrible. That's the least that can be said. When the believers came to the church in Zagreb, when the congregation rallied, they were under threat. The Croats gathered together and members of paramilitaries issued threats to them. They wrote on the churches, "Srbe na vrbe," "Hang Serbs on trees," and other threats of that kind. And at the time in the government we had the testimonies of people that were recorded whereby the church premises or church yards were used as toilets. So can you imagine a situation like that? When people saw that, they didn't like coming to church because their lives were at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who were the exponents of the most extreme behaviour against the Serbs at the time? What social group?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I don't want to speak about groups. Groups were incited, and the state organs allowed them to behave the way they did. Everybody knows that from 1990 to 1991, a lot of people arrived in Croatia who were listed as fascists and terrorists everywhere in the world. For example, the murderer of the Yugoslav ambassador in Sweden, Rolovic, returned to Croatia. His name was Miro Barisic. Then in Dalmatia, Pavelic suddenly turned up, pretending to be a fighter for human rights. He was one of the survivors of the group in 1970 who had been sent from Australia to raise a rebellion in Yugoslavia, and unfortunately, they began their activities on Mount Radusa, where I was born. Such people became esteemed in Croatia, and the media reported that Franjo Tudjman liked to meet those people on his visits to the USA, Germany, and other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about Ustasha emigres who then returned to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were emigres who had inherited the fascist ideology, or the Nazi ideology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the relationship between the return of those emigres and the formation of the army, and how much of it was open and how much of it was concealed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The Croats did nothing covertly. They were proud of what they were doing. They were proud that people were returning to Croatia who could assist in the establishing of a Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did they begin forming those famous volunteer units on a large scale?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: In 1990, in Croatia, a secret import of weapons began. I think that in these tabs there is a lot of information about that. Unfortunately, these weapons were imported into Croatia secretly from several European countries. I don't want to disparage European countries, and I don't want to say that their police and military organs didn't know about this import of weapons to arm units in friendly Yugoslavia. That's what all European countries used to say about our country. There was a plan, that is, which extended beyond the borders of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the National Guard Corps? Can you answer that briefly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was modelled after the Ustasha formations of 1941 and the so-called National Guard of 1939 when the autonomous unit called the Croatian Banovina was formed in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, and when many Serb territories were included in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 4, we have a document that you brought here which illustrates what you've just been saying. It's from the command of the 1st Military District. It's dated August 1990, and the date is the 27th of August, 1990.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at what it says in the first paragraph. It says: "On the 18th of August, 1990, the presence of over a hundred persons from these countries has been registered. This refers to Canada, Australia, and the USA. Among them, several members of leaderships of certain extremist organisations have been identified. These people are on the list of Yugoslav citizens who are to be arrested if they attempt to enter the country."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is not translated. Put it on --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can put it on the ELMO, just page 1, just to see what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the arrival of emigres. You mentioned criminals. Would you read the second half of the first paragraph and tell us what the date is here. Can we see the date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can see the date here. This is a document dated the 27th of August, 1990. So that's very early on. And it's actually preparation for what was to follow. The Yugoslav organs knew, and that's the saddest thing about this, because anywhere else all the people on this list would have been arrested. And I hope that Interpol would have helped if any of them had escaped. But because the members of the Yugoslav Presidency from Croatia and Slovenia had a strong influence there and they advocated separatism, this information was provided only to a narrow circle of politicians and offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is mention here of the presence on the 18th of August, 1990, at a rally of the HDZ in Sarajevo. Can you see this in the first paragraph? So they were actually staying in Sarajevo, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and these persons whose names are listed in the footnote are mentioned, and they should have been arrested but nobody arrested them.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, now, tell us, was there any connection between those paramilitary units set up in Croatia and the Muslim side, which was also creating some sort of paramilitary units at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I hope the Presiding Judge will forgive me, but I have to go back to World War II when the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina were declared to be the flowers of the Croatian nation. Franjo Tudjman, which with the HDZ wanted to cut off Bosnia and Herzegovina together with the Muslims from Yugoslavia and create a greater Croatia, such as Hitler had created in 1941. And it was sickening to see those rallies in Bosnia and Herzegovina where the Croatian and Muslims' flags were tied together and the Serbian flag was nowhere to be seen, even though up to 20 or 30 years before the Serbs had been the majority population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, amounting to 64 per cent. They owned 64 per cent of the land, that is. They were the owners of the new state, but yet the Croats and the Muslims together wanted to separate it from Yugoslavia, and probably they were planning the same fate for the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina that the Serbs had suffered in the Croatian towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the import of weapons. This has already been documented before this Tribunal, so I will not document it again. However, there is a very interesting document here in tab 5, and it refers to the 13th of February, 1991. It's a note about talks between the federal secretary, Budimir Loncar, with the state secretary of the MIP of the Republic of Hungary on the 11th of February, 1991, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is not translated. If you wish to cite a particular portion, then we can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Put it on the ELMO. First page 1 and then page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First I want to clarify with the witness: Do you know who Budimir Loncar was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes; he was my boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was your boss, but was he the minister of foreign affairs of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a cadre from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and a representative of Croatia in the federal government. Who was the president of the federal -- who was the federal Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It was Ante Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So the Croat Ante Markovic was the Prime Minister; Budimir Loncar, a Croat, was the minister of foreign affairs, and he was having talks with the minister of foreign affairs of Hungary.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And what we see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just let's have a look at it because I want to go through the document. On page 1, in the last paragraph, what does it say? Would you read it, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Page 1, last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: "First the incident erupted because of deliveries of weapons to the organs in Croatia from Hungarian military reserves which is against the mutual agreement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, sorry to interrupt you, but we must take the break now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, please look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the middle of this first paragraph, which is very long, the minister of foreign affairs says to his Hungarian colleague: "The delivery of weapons from Hungary under such conditions represents sabotage." That's what he tells his colleague. And several lines lower down, he says -- read it: "We have always said that --"

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: "We have always said that our relations with Hungary are ideal. This consignment of weapons, however, has caused unease in Yugoslavia as well as reactions in Hungary, especially in the parliament."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, please go on to the next paragraph, where it says: "But --"

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: "But solving this based on discovery of the full truth can be useful to both sides. Whether the ministers will remain in the government or not is an internal matter for Hungary, but we want to know what their responsibility is."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So a lot of questions were asked here as to whether the information about the legal import of weapons from Hungary was true. This is a conversation between the SFRY minister of foreign affairs with the minister -- his counterpart in Hungary about this, this occurrence.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If you remember, and the Chamber will also probably remember, when referring to these events I said that one should not underestimate or disparage European countries and that these weapons illegally imported into Croatia could not have gone past their police and immigration organs unnoticed. So this is a conversation between two ministers. The weapons were, therefore, brought into Croatia and this was organised by a friendly neighbouring country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at page 3.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Delivery of weapons from Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 3, third paragraph from the bottom, Loncar says, "We don't want the problem we are discussing to be discussed in the OSCE forums."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milosevic. The third page is missing from my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then I will read from my copy. Only one passage that I'll quote. At the bottom of page 3 - I hope the others have it - in the last paragraph, end of last paragraph, the state secretary of Hungary says: "The Hungarian government has stated in public that this is regrettable and that the government -- that it has nothing to do with the Hungarian minority in Yugoslavia or its organisations." So they say that this event is regrettable. That's the position of the Hungarian government. In the same tab, further on, there is some information. Would you please just take a look at it. It has to do with involvement of foreign factors in the illegal import of weapons into Yugoslavia in October 1990 to January 1991. That's the time period.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 1, under A, from Hungary.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, here it is again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it mention 20.000 automatic rifles, 7.62, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It says that the transport was carried out --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter which company transported the goods.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's important because the company's a Croatian one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's understood. There's no need to prove it. And then it goes on to talk about this from Hungary, and then further on it says everything from Hungary, the 18th, the 16th, the 7th of December, when seven persons were arrested at the civilian airport in Budapest on the 7th of December 1991, and then it goes on to talk about the 19th of December 1991 when a large quantity of projectiles were transported from Hungary to Croatia. Then there is mention of weapons from Germany, from Austria, and other countries. So is this large-scale illegal import of weapons into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina had this information in 1992 and 1993 for as long as the Krajina lasted, and here one can see that what I said when answering one of your previous questions, the intention towards Yugoslavia and the Serbs extended beyond the borders of Croatia. It was no accident that criminals from so many different countries could bring weapons into Croatia without the knowledge of their state organs. As we can see in this conversation between two ministers, one from Yugoslavia and the other one from Hungary, this has been confirmed. This document also mentions Austria and Germany. They wanted to break up Yugoslavia, and that was at the root of all the misfortunes that occurred later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We can see that this happened in 1990 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this has to do with that question of yours, because you keep the asking about the indictment. In the indictment, where individual criminal responsibility is mentioned, it follows that what happened was a consequence of a policy or a plan of mine, my behaviour, the behaviour of Serbia and so on, but it's evident from everything there is that it was a consequence of the policy of armed secession and the self-organisation of the Serbian people in Croatia for purposes of self-defence. The fact that individual crimes happened in all this, nobody denies that, although I can't confirm it either because I don't know everything that happened, but the cause and effect links are evident. There was no joint criminal enterprise on the Serbian side. On the contrary. This wave which began even before 1990 with expulsions and murders of Serbs and all the other cruelty they suffered throughout this period, and it culminated in armed secession and the consequences of armed secession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry, Mr. Jarcevic, I omitted to go through a few tabs before this tab number 5. So just for the sake of the documents themselves, I would like to put a very technical question to you in order to be able to tender the documents that we've gone through already. Please, in tab 1 -- it's pretty late. Let's go through this as fast as we can. What is in tab 1? Take a look at this. What is this? On page 25 of this document there is a circle that is Wednesday, the 3rd of March. It says: "[In English] The radioactive waste management in the area of Croatia affected by war - Damir Subasic, Antun Stare, Marjan Gunaric," et cetera. [Interpretation] And so on. In parenthesis, "Croatia." What does this document say? And later on, you have documents and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is an international conference on mixed waste and environment restoration held in Tucson, Arizona. However, something that precedes this document is far more important, and I hope that the Trial Chamber will not mind if I say a few words about this. Much earlier in Pecs in Hungary, yet another international conference was held about radioactive waste as well. In 1991, the Croatian delegation there presented a report stating that certain areas in Croatia will be used for storing radioactive waste and chemical poison. The maps that show where this storage will be overlap with the Serb settlements there that were fully cleansed ethnically in 1991 and the villages were razed to the ground, including the infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
