utterances.text: All right, Mr. Jarcevic. In order to use time as efficiently as possible, are these documents that show that radioactive material, as envisaged by the Croatian authorities, should be stored in areas where Serbs lived?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And also, may I remind you of the fact that in 1991 the Serbs were totally expelled from that area, Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, could this tab number 1 be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, what's not clear to me at the moment is what this tab actually is. Does it relate to the Tucson conference or does it relate to the Hungary conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. These are two conferences independent from one another. One was in Hungary, one was in the United States, geographically speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does the document relate to both of them?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document has to do with the first conference in Hungary, with maps as to where radioactive waste is to be deposited. We only have the programme of the conference from the United States of America, and it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the first page is the programme of the conference in the US?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then, under number 7, we see the radioactive waste management in the area of Croatia affected by --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only topic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We see that. And the second document has to do with the conference in Hungary.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this map that shows the sites coincides with the map of the area from where Serbs were expelled.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Precisely. Can I say what document is missing here, and if you're prepared to hear me out, I'll tell you what this has to do with that. The route of this radioactive material was from Germany to Slavonski Brod by train, and then it was put onto trucks and taken to its final destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could tab 1 please be admitted into evidence, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see any relevance with this trial, this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are not with you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. We consider it to be relevant. We'll admit it. Yes. A number for the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibits with the binder accompanying -- I'm sorry, the binder will be Exhibit D338. And the tabs dealt with thus far, which are 16, 17, 4, 5, and 1, are admitted as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is this in tab 2? In all fairness, in part of one of your answers to one of my questions, you spoke about two peoples, two nations in Croatia. So what is this in tab 2? I see it's January 2006, the parliamentary Assembly of --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The Council of Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- the Council of Europe.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is very interesting, and I hope that it will interest the Trial Chamber too. The parliament and government of the Serb Krajina in exile have been working, and they've registered three offices of theirs in France, Canada, and Holland before they opened their offices in some other European countries too. They consulted politicians and parliamentarians from European parliaments, and they were surprised that in 1990 the civil war and the persecution of the Serbs started with the change in the status of Croatia. Twenty-eight MPs from the parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe signed a declaration stating that Croatia should give Serbs the same status that they had in 1990, that is to say that constitutionally Croatia be regulated as a bi-national state, like Belgium, or a tri-national state, like Britain, or a quadri-national state, like Switzerland. This will be on the agenda of the Council of Europe in April, and even more parliamentarians are going to support the mentioned 28, and they will vote in favour of a resolution which will be more binding than a declaration. At the same time, a few MPs from European countries this summer, before the European parliament - that is to say the parliament of the European Union - they are going to sponsor a similar resolution and they're going to ask Croatia to do what I've just said, and in this way there will be conditions placed on its admission into the European Union. They will not be able to accede before they give the Serbs back the status they had in 1990 and before that. I should like to say that we have parliamentarians from the major countries of Europe, they are going to sponsor this; Britain, France, Italy and Belgium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance, Mr. Robinson, is in the fact that obviously judging by these reactions, too, the decision taken in 1990 for the Serbs to be abolished as a people or nation in Croatia cannot be considered a fait accompli. It is a pending issue, and it will probably remain a pending issue before this decision, which was highly discriminatory and which went against the grain of all relevant principles and norms, is finally annulled. As you can see, even 15 years after that, it is brought up yet again even in the Council of Europe and in the European parliament, as Mr. Jarcevic has been saying. So it has to do with the presence of - how should I put this not to use a stronger term? - an unjust phenomenon that marked the beginning of the 1990s and the persecution of Serbs in part of Europe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is not relevant. We'll not admit it. Please move on to another matter, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us just go through tab 3 as well. What is there in tab 3, Mr. Jarcevic? This is a document from September 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This one is not translated, so let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this information about -- what does it say here? It says: "Recent knowledge about activities of the members of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia, the stay of extremist emigres, the training of members of the 'Croatian army.'" What does this document speak of? This is a document of the secretariat, the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. As briefly as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document is similar to the ones that pertain to the import of weapons in terms of what it caused it and what it was supposed to cause. It didn't cause anything. As we've said, in any other country people like this would have been arrested or at least prevented from taking any kind of action. In view of the fact that the Presidency consisted of representatives --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We are not going into all of that now, Mr. Jarcevic. This document talks about the stay of extremist emigres and what kind of knowledge existed about that, and then you testified about extremist emigres and the beginning of violence, physical violence against Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that is correct, we've already spoken about that, but what I'm saying is that in any other country they would have been arrested or prevented from taking any kind of activity. Now, why was that not done in Yugoslavia in 1990? That is a question that is very interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now tab 4 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted into evidence, because it talks about extremist emigres, and all of that serves the purposes of the escalation of violence against the Serbs. So the year is 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The information the 1st Military District. What does that contain? As briefly as possible. It's the 4th of November, 1991 the transference of military weapons and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and been through it in some detail.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, just briefly, let's go through tab 8, Mr. Jarcevic, and tell us what that contains, and a short explanation will suffice, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just an inquiry. Tab 4, we have discussed tab 4, but that's a document from the 27th of August, 1990, and it's not a document of the 4th of November, 1991. So I wonder whether there is something in disorder, because I can't see that we have discussed any document from November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I can. Probably Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff might have misheard when I referred to tab 7, which relates to the 14th of November, 1991, and the transference of military materiel and parts of the weapons, whereas tab 4 is August 1990, but tab 7 is November 1991. As far as I understood it, you said that it was adopted, admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You haven't reached tab 7. Did you deal with tab 7, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeated it now, but since you've said that I dealt with tab 7, then -- no, I didn't deal with it, but you said that I didn't need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are getting confused. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, your point related to tab 4. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff was speaking about tab 4, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He was speaking of tab 7, but we were thinking tab 4. So I think he did not deal with tab 7 yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the problem, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So you're now going to deal with tab 7.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that there is no need for me to go back to tab 4. Tab 4 was the 27th of August, 1990, and we've done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tab 7 is November 1991, and it speaks of the transfer of military equipment and other weapons of foreign origin to the territory of Posusje in order to equip the paramilitary units. And that is a document of the 1st Military District of the JNA at that time. Now, what does it speak of? What's this tab about, this particular document, Mr. Jarcevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean tab 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 7.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It says tab 8 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We're dealing with tab 7 now. Tab 8 is another tab. Tab 7 is a document of the 1st Military District relating to the transfer of military equipment and other weapons of foreign origin to equip the paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this contains everything that we were speaking about so far. There are facts about how paramilitaries were armed. However, these paramilitaries are not disarmed, being disarmed, that nothing was done against the organisers of their arming, that is to say nothing was done to prevent arms reaching from them -- reaching them. And I say that because in the organs of the federation, there were many, and they were people in positions of decision-making, who assisted activities of this kind in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document, please, Mr. Robinson, tab 7?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, in tab 8 we have a document of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior. Can we see that on the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is the date of that document, the Croatian ministry?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The 17th of January, 1991. And since it is a report or record intended for the federal organs -- the document deals with the distribution of weapons to paramilitary units, and the types of weapons are mentioned - Kalashnikovs, and so on and so forth - but this document didn't help prevent what Croatia was doing to the Serbs that year and the following year, although the signatory is the minister of the interior of Croatia, Josip Boljkovac. He saw no reason not to sign this together with the federal secretary, and nothing happened. Nobody questioned it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd like to tender this document too, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should say that all these documents are not translated. They're marked for identification pending translation. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, in addition to that, it is, of course, for me not possible to cross-examine on these documents because I have no idea really what is said in there. And in addition to that, the witness has told us that he was actually at that time not in Croatia. He was living, as I understood him, in Serbia. I can't really see how he relates to this document and how he confirms the contents of these documents. I can't -- at the moment I cannot see any relation of him to those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the witness was very much informed about everything that went on there, because he was politically involved in it all. He was the minister of the -- he was foreign minister of Krajina very shortly afterwards, and he couldn't have become minister of Krajina by just having his name looked up in the telephone directory. He was a man who had already worked in the field and helped solve current political problems, the ones that existed. So he is fully informed about what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it. We'll mark it for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would find it helpful, when you have got so few documents as there are in this instance compared with so many others, if you had somebody here who was able to tell you if there was anything in them that required cross-examination, but perhaps today you don't have that facility which you often do have.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, part of the documents I had available when I prepared for the cross-examination, and of course our staff member who speaks the language told me what it is, but we actually received these documents -- at least, some of these documents I see today for the first time, and therefore I didn't get any information what it could be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the position with these documents and their translation or their non-translation? Why are they not translated?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know that exactly. As far as I'm concerned, I considered that they had been translated when I received them in the binder. Now I hear that they haven't been translated. I assume there's a technical reason. It might be a mistake on the part of my associates. I don't exclude that at all. But I really did believe that the documents that I have here and that arrived here had been translated. But as you can see, they are very few in number and short documents. So they're not long documents, and you can identify them very easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, nonetheless, the Prosecutor is at a disadvantage. How is she to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what we have already seen shown on the overhead projector and from what the interpreters have already interpreted and said, you can see quite easily what these documents relate to, and anything that is questionable there or that can be challenged is quite easy to see. But it's not the practice that I suggest be introduced, it's the practice that was introduced on many occasions by the other side over there as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, which ones do you not have any information about?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It was actually the military documents that were now the last ones. I had information on these talks about the arming of the Croats. That I had already, and I know what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us which tab numbers, then, you don't have any information?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would have to compare them now with the B/C/S version that I have in the other binder that I got originally. I only see that the military documents I didn't have. Those -- I mean, tab 7 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, 4 is a military document as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. But I would have to check now. I only notice that some of them I've never seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We need a little bit more time because it's even more confusing than I thought because the original tab numbers that I had in the binder have -- are now completely different tabs. So that comes in addition to this, but Ms. Dicklich is just checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to this point, Mr. Milosevic. Continue. That one is also marked for identification pending its translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, take a look at tab 9 now, please, which is information. What does it say? What kind of information is this? Can you find your way around those documents?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please. Microphone for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, a subject we were discussing, the illegal introduction of weapons into Croatia. Here we have it again. The 31st of August, 1991 is the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, Mr. President, but the interesting thing to note here is this, and every citizen of Yugoslavia could have seen that, and people from the world, too, what was -- this was about a flight by an aeroplane which was full of weapons for the Croatian military, and the plane was piloted by a Croatian emigre from Canada, but the company -- the plane belonged to a Uganda company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was rented out.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I have a document here with a Nigerian -- from the Nigerian embassy so I thought it was Nigeria, but it was Uganda, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was a large plane, a Boeing 707, in fact.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and it was grounded by the Yugoslav People's Army planes at Pleso airport in Zagreb. It was forcibly ground, forced to land.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say? What was its destination according to documents? The third paragraph: "The Boeing set out from Uganda with its destination Burnik near Ljubljana."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The fact that Croatia and Slovenia or their air forces at the time worked together to break up Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Their forces, interpreter's correction, not air forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did the -- this Croatian emigre say? He says it in the last paragraph. In talking to the official organs of the Yugoslav People's Army, what did he say? The last paragraph on page 1 of this report.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to read it out? "In initial talk with the official organs of the Yugoslav People's Army, Kikes said that the president of the Socialist Croatian Businessmen's and Intellectuals Alliance in Toronto had 225 members and that all the leading members of that society were members of the Croatian Democratic Union, and so on. According to Kikes, the society had amassed together 880.000 dollars for the arming of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia. The money was deposited in a bank in Klagenfurt, Austria, already on the 22nd of August this year."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say at the end of that first paragraph on page 2, towards the end of that first paragraph? It says it should have been taken over by who?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: By the government -- a representative of the government of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then what does it say in the next paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Kikes, in this first statement of his, was adamant that the purchase of weapons were intended for the Republic of Croatia and that behind this whole action was the Croatian Democratic Union."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does it say after that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: "During the day the forces of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia surrounded Pleso airport in Zagreb and used mortar fire to try and destroy the plane belonging to the Uganda company with the illegally purchased and illegally transported weapons and military equipment and materiel of foreign production, foreign make. The JNA units -- or, rather, the JNA unit providing security for the airport retaliated by firing at a -- destroyed a vehicle of the attacker. Through the actions of the forces of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia this was stopped for the time being."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document into evidence as well now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a document dated August 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's admitted on the same terms, marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 10, you have a document of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence. It's signed by the deputy federal secretary for national defence, Stane Brovet. It concerns information about the import of weapons and military equipment from Hungary, and it's dated the 10th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We see here that as of the 20th of August until the 9th of September 1991, weapons were being transported into Croatia by planes belonging to agricultural estates, so that the import of weapons was not ceasing. As the ministry established long before, neighbouring countries were deeply involved, unfortunately, in arming these paramilitary units which were to cause the suffering of millions of people in Yugoslavia. When I say millions, I mean all Yugoslavs, because there were sanctions, and industrial and other facilities were destroyed, so that the suffering is still going on in all the republics which are now independent states.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have received information that these military documents were handed over for translation on the 13th of February. That is two weeks ago. They're short military documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I can't allow that to go without comment, because two weeks is not enough notice, not enough time for the Translation Unit, as you well know. They should have been sent in at least a month before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'm informing you of the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But it's not sufficient to inform me of the fact. What I'm pointing out to you is that you have been delinquent in submitting the documents to the Translation Unit late, and that is why we are in the position which we now face today. And you must attend to these matters. It is within the discretion of the Chamber not to allow you to lead evidence on a document which is not translated. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at tab 11. It's a letter from the Federal Secretariat of National Defence to the Prime Minister of Croatia, dated the 30th of August, 1991. So this is communication between the Ministry of Defence and the Prime Minister of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This shows the third source of arming the paramilitary formations of Croatia. A train was attacked which was transporting weapons belonging to the JNA on the Zagreb-Belgrade line. Of course I assume that those who are responsible for this were arrested and tried, but I never heard that they actually were. The Croatian leadership, I assume, should have been punished, but I don't know that anything was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was this about? In point 1 it says: "On the Zagreb-Belgrade line --"

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "-- military equipment was taken from the wagon which was being transported from the Republic of Slovenia pursuant to a decision of the Presidency of the SFRY." So the JNA was leaving Slovenia. Its trains had to pass through Croatia where they were stopped and looted.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that what this document says?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence is writing this to the Croatian Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As there's no translation into English, you have faithfully translated what it says here. The JNA, which was declared an aggressor in Slovenia, was pulling out, pursuant to a decision of the Presidency, passing through Croatia, which was a part of the then-Yugoslavia. However, Croatian paramilitary formations ambushed the trains, looted them, and the participants of this robbery would have been punished and tried in any country, but in Yugoslavia nothing happened because in the top leadership of the then-Yugoslavia the dominant role was played for the most part by cadres from Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And what does it say in paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It says that ten rail wagons of various quartermaster material was looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that established?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes it was. There's no need for me to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is no need to comment. What does it say in paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It says at 0640 hours on the 30th of August, 1991, a train carrying military equipment was stopped in the village of Mrkovci. That's close to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, and what about the next paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It says it's occurring more and more frequently that military columns are being stopped by force or trains with military equipment stopped and members of the JNA maltreated. Military equipment and property is regularly being confiscated and the extent of all this is overstepping all reasonable limits. It cannot be tolerated. And this is happening even after --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be a pause between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just a minute, please. The interpreter is asking the witness and yourself to observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for the campaign started in mid-June 1990 in Croatia in connection with the replacement of cadres in the Territorial Defence, do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the Territorial Defence of Croatia and in Croatian police stations, as early as 1990 there was replacement of people who were Serbs, and of course people were brought in their place who were supposed to carry out orders from Zagreb which were aimed at the ethnic cleansing of Serbs. This was soon to be demonstrated after these dismissals, and it was to culminate in 1990 and 1991, as seen in the Secretary-General's report in the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look, please. At that time, you said that at that time there was a lot of arson and so on. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, look at tab 13. It's a letter from the Ministry of Interior of the Zadar police administration. It's dated 2001.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document is very important. I hope that the Chamber will understand this, because it was compiled after the civil war in 2001. I wish to remind everybody that this kind of report has to be submitted in every trial in which ethnic Serbs have instituted a suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "In connection with your request of the number and date above, we hereby submit the following information: During 1990 --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Don't comment, just read.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: "During 1991 --" Well, I'm trying to say that this is an organ of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in Zadar, in the area, 21 fires and explosions were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: PU is the police administration?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in 1990, the Zadar police administration recorded in its area a total of 21 arsons and explosions.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't say here who planted the bombs, but had the Serbs done that they would certainly have said that. It goes on to say: "With the spreading of war activities in these areas, the number of fires and explosions increased so that in 1991 381 instances were recorded, whereas in 1992 a total of 673 instances of fires or explosions were recorded." I want to say that it was only Serb property and only Serb houses that were blown up or set fire to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While in Zadar and the area there were no Serb units and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is something that can be tendered into evidence, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, do you by any chance know that -- who sent this information to whom and for what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In trials before the court in Zadar, this kind of document is delivered to Serb prosecutors who gave this to me, to the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in exile, and I felt duty-bound to give the Court this information which comes from police sources in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So do you know to what court was this document submitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the court in Zadar, the municipal court in Zadar. You can ask the Croatian side, if I may make so bold as to suggest it, for all this documentation accompanying this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know who was tried at that court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some individuals sued the Croatian state. Others sued Zadar municipality, and some sued the insurance company where the building they owned which was destroyed was insured. As you know, there is more than one way to initiate civil court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can see here that the memorandum of the Ministry of the Interior, the Zadar police administration is the heading on this letter, and it's addressed to the Zadar municipal court.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the municipal court in Zadar, informing the court that in 1990 there were 21 instances of fires or explosions; in 1991, 381; and in 1992, 673. So this is being sent from the Zadar police administration to the court in Zadar in connection with certain lawsuits initiated by Serbs before that court. And I assume that the court in Zadar asked the Zadar police for this information and this is the response they received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to your information, this is precisely one of the documents that we did not receive in advance but only today, and it's about another six documents that we only got today. Just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This one is very short.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, and I will actually use it, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In parallel with the declaration of secession of Croatia and all the events you've been testifying about up to now, were any peace negotiations being carried on that you know about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, with my arrival in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, this coincided with the negotiations which went on until the summer of 1994. Throughout 1993, due to circumstances because of my office, I attended all these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you attended all the negotiations that Krajina had with the Croatian side and international mediators?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Better to say they were organised by members of the international community, members of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, and on two occasions representatives of the government of the USA and the Russian Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the international mediators or the representatives of the USA and Russia put forward proposals to both sides or was it just the two sides talking to each other? Could you describe the negotiations a little bit.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: As the standpoints of the government of the Krajina and the government of Croatia were diametrically opposed and at the first meeting each side would present its standpoint, the people I have just mentioned mediated, the people from the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia and on two occasions representatives from Russia and America. Most often, when we could not agree, they would propose the text of an agreement we were supposed to sign. I cannot generalise here, but every point had to be discussed separately. Let me clarify. For example, the negotiations in New York in February, those in Geneva in March, April, and all the way up to June, the ones in Erdut, the secret negotiations in Norway, the secret negotiations in Great Britain, each had different characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you were one the chief protagonists in these negotiations on the Serb side, I would like to go through them all in chronological order. So please be kind enough to tell us what characterised the negotiations in February. After that, you will go on to those in March and later. I will ask you what was happening on the ground at the same time as these negotiations were going on. Please go in chronological order. So let's look at February first.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: February 1993, New York. It was Mr. Cyrus Vance who was chairing these negotiations. David Owen was there as well. And the third person was Gert Ahrends, who I mentioned a while ago and I told you that he spoke excellent Serbia, and also a lawyer by the name of Okun. I cannot remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ambassador Okun was secretary to Mr. Cyrus Vance?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: That was the group that we were meeting with, and at that time, because of the Croatian offensive on the 22nd of January 1993 against Ravni Kotari and the Maslenica bridge, I don't remember exactly how many people were killed there, but the number is about 300, it was very hard for the representatives of the Krajina to sit opposite the Croatian delegation, so Cyrus Vance and David Owen decided that they should sit in one room and we in another one. Then they would bring the positions of one delegation to the other and the other way around. I don't know whether I've put this very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's get this clear. At that time these were areas under UN protection.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did the Croatian offensive take place again these parts of UN protected areas?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The 22nd of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So for a year, or a bit less than that, those were UN protected areas?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. At least half a year later, after the UN forces were deployed on the ground, this Croatian offensive took place.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, before that there was yet another offensive, an attack on the Republic of the Serb Krajina, or a UN protected area, and that was at 21st of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did that happen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: At the Miljevac plateau in Dalmatia. And all the detained soldiers of the Serb Krajina were killed there or, rather, all of them who were there, who happened to be there. I cannot tell you about this exactly, but this should really cause surprise all round. The Croats asked UNPROFOR officers to convey to the Krajina government and the General Staff that one of the coastal towns will be hosting an international children's festival and that the Serbs should refrain from shooting or any other kind of incidents. Of course the Serbs, as always, heeded this. They relaxed and the Croats took advantage of that. They broke in and killed everybody in the garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then Ravni Kotari --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are again overlapping. The interpreter is asking you to observe the pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, under these circumstances, who was it that invited you to New York?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: We were invited to New York by Cedric Thornberry. He got us ready and set the date for when we should go. The delegation of the Republic of Serb Krajina was led by the president, Goran Hadzic. He was accompanied by Mile Paspalj, president of the parliament, and I as foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Cedric Thornberry was --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- the civilian head of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he sent you to New York, the delegation that you mentioned just now. And who was there on the Croatian side? You've already said that the international intermediaries were there; Vance, Owen, and the people who worked for them.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time we did not see the Croatian delegation, but Slavko Degoricija led the Croatian delegation. He also led the Croatian delegation at the negotiations in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened in New York that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: In New York -- I'm sorry, I know that I've moved on too fast yet again, so I do apologise to the interpreters. Since the international mediators let the delegation of the Serb Krajina know that they considered them to be uncooperative, at the first meeting Mr. Hadzic said that -- that he will let Croatia use Peruca, Zelenik, and the Maslenica Bridge, and he said that because the Croats explained in great detail over their media that the Serbs would not allow the Maslenica bridge to be used and that Croatia had no possibility of conducting transport and pursuing tourism through that part of Dalmatia and Lika. They had to do all of that by ship, and that was expensive. And of course in that way they were actually turning their own population against the Serbs. That is why, through President Hadzic, we offered these three facilities to the Croatian state so that they could use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was concluded in New York? And what did the international envoys propose in addition to your own attempt to show how cooperative you were? What did the international mediators have to say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time they just brought in the Croatian plan. At that time, Croatia, like once in 1992 before I joined the government of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, they had a proposal to give Serbs self-government only in two municipalities; Glina and Knin. In order to be clear on this, that was the area of one-third of the Republic of the Serb Krajina. Of course that was not serious. And that plan would remain as one of the Croatian trump cards all the way up to 1995. And regrettably, the US ambassador brought this plan that was anything but serious to Knin in 1995, and he proclaimed it to be his own proposal, called Z-4. However, that was the same plan that was put forth to us by the Croats in 1992 and also in New York when I was a member of the Krajina delegation. Of course, we did not want to accept that and the talks failed, as the intermediaries told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, are you referring to the continuation of the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You had these negotiations in New York. They failed. It was February 1993. And when were the next negotiations held and who participated in them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The international mediators indeed realised by then that this Croatian plan was unbelievably unacceptable. It lacked seriousness. So these municipalities that the Croats were talking about were even smaller than in the former Yugoslavia. And mostly in the Serbian settlements in Slavonia, in Western Srem, even those Serb settlements would become automatically part of Croatia. We tried to talk about this in March again, and then in June, I think, in Geneva, and I think that, in the meantime, we met three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to what you said just now about the Miljevac plateau and the attack of the Croatian forces at the UN protected area in the territory of the Republic of Serb Krajina, in relation to that was anything said in Security Council Resolution 762?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, all these Resolutions have already been admitted, so I don't think there's any need for me to present them yet again this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Croatia was not condemned at all in that Resolution, and that's what happened in all the Resolutions that followed, regardless of the kind of crimes committed by Croatia against the Serbs or inhabitants of UN protected areas. The only thing that would be written would be that Croatia had to withdraw their troops from the Miljevac plateau. And of course the Croats only gave their soldiers police uniforms and kept them there as a police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So what was the situation in actual fact? They attacked the Miljevac plateau, the Security Council says that they should withdraw their soldiers, which did not happen, and the Security Council is cautioning both sides, telling them to exercise restraint. Was this the customary phraseology used when Serbs are attacked, then both sides are cautioned to exercise restraint?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was the recommendation given to both sides, to exercise restraint. That was so insulting for the Serb side and the Republic of Serb Krajina, because our army never crossed the border of Croatia, never attacked the population. I'm sorry, just one more thing. Even in reports sent to the Security Council that had to do with these events, the terminology was not changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In what sense are you saying this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Croatia was never condemned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened then at the next round of negotiations, and where was that held?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The next negotiations were held in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: From March to June. I think there were three rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: February, New York; the next month --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again the interpreter is asking please speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The international mediators explained this by stating that it was less expensive if we met in Geneva rather than in New York. There was no other reason presented for changing the venue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Never mind. Geneva, New York. Who participated in these negotiations in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: In Geneva it was Goran Hadzic again and the president of the parliament, Mile Paspalj. I was there with them, and they were a bit different from the ones in New York, because we and the Croats both agreed to sit at a big round table in a single room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us what happened then.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: There was a repetition of what happened in New York. Slavko Degoricija yet again offered Serbs self-government only in two districts. Of course the delegation of the Republic of Serb Krajina could not accept that and it proposed that we include in a possible agreement the entire Republic of the Serb Krajina. The international mediators accepted this idea of ours in the hope that, through subsequent economic trade, cultural, and educational relations, they would perhaps turn Croatia into something that would, in 1995, be achieved in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say a single state consisting of two entities. So that is what was heard all the time in Geneva. And then in Erdut on the 15th and 16th of July, 1995, this was materialised. The government of the United States of America and the government of Russia intervened then, and their representatives, their deputy foreign ministers, were present when the Erdut agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the proposal of the international mediators in Geneva? In order to save time, the negotiations went on from March to June, but these were not three different, separate topics. It was an attempt to find a solution. Would that be it, roughly, the substance of these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. An agreement was supposed to be reached that would be accepted by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that until then the main difference was that they proposed an autonomy for Knin and Glina, whereas you proposed autonomy for all of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: We suggested that there be no break-up of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the position of the international mediators?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The position of the international mediators was in favour of our position, because they realised that their proposal really lacked seriousness, and that would figure yet again in the so-called Z-4 plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The Croatian side proposed autonomy to you and one-third of the territory of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're asking for the entire territory of Krajina to be taken into account, and the international mediators consider that to be logical?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the situation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the reaction of the international mediators or, rather, what was the reaction of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness, if you just took the opportunity to listen to the interpreter, you'd be very sorry for her. She's going at breakneck pace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, Mr. Milosevic said that Security Council Resolution 762 had been admitted already, but I'm not sure whether it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We'd have to check that through Harland's evidence. I think he was the witness the Prosecutor used to bring in the various UN documents. We'll check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time, and were the Court thinking of adjourning soon can I draw to your attention the following: The order you made on the 15th of February was that the accused should provide more information on his witness list, and you said for the next four to six weeks. There's been a short exchange of correspondence. The Chamber may be aware of that. The present position is we've been notified of this witness, who was to last six hours. That's -- six hours, I think, and one other witness for this week, and no other. Was it six hours? Three hours, sorry. Three hours for this witness, so he could have finished today, tomorrow's witness could have finished tomorrow. We've been given no notification of a further witness for this week nor has there been any compliance with the four to six weeks order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the explanation for this? Why have you only notified two or three witnesses when I specifically instructed that you should notify witnesses for the next four to six weeks?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Nice said, after Mr. Jarcevic, there is yet another witness, and after that witness Momir Bulatovic is supposed to testify, who had been announced a long time ago. Last week, I asked the liaison officer to expedite matters to get him here as soon as possible, and I received assurances that he would be brought in as soon as possible. I did not conduct any additional checks this morning, but my understanding was that he would arrive only on Wednesday. In view of the fact that I have not seen him for several years now, I need to talk to Mr. Bulatovic before his testimony, because it will go on for quite a while. So he cannot start testifying on Wednesday. There aren't any other working days until the end of this week, and then there's next week. So I assume that during the course of that week and the next week I would be able to proof Mr. Bulatovic and that he could start testifying next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are being too clever by half. You haven't really answered my question. You must provide a list of your witnesses for the next four to six weeks. Mr. Bulatovic, I understand, will take some time, but not all the time. So I expect you to carry out the instructions of the Trial Chamber. We will adjourn for 20 minutes. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, to answer Judge Kwon's question, it was produced through Branko Kostic. It's D333, tab 81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, before I go on, here is a list in English. It was prepared several days ago. I haven't managed to find out why it wasn't submitted to you, but I will give it to the liaison officer. It's already been submitted in electronic form to the other side, and it's the witness list for the next few weeks. I would like to ask you to solve as soon as possible the issue of your order that Clinton and Clark testify. It's very important to me for planning purposes. As for everything else, I will inform you later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As you well know, we only received the written submissions on that last week, in the latter part of last week, and we will give a decision by the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I've been telling you about this request of mine for more than two years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the purpose of a comment like that? You very well know that we were not in a position to deal with it in the absence of written submissions, and we only received those in the latter part of last week from the assigned counsel. Don't waste time, and don't be mischievous. Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I assume that you understand how important these witnesses are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, in these events that you've been testifying about, including the negotiations you've spoken about, what was the relationship of the Serbs in Krajina or, rather, their attitude toward the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Vance-Owen Plan was accepted in the hope that it would be implemented. It contained two provisions guaranteeing this: First, that there would be no prejudging of the political solution at stake; and secondly, on the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina or the UN protected areas, Yugoslav laws would be implemented. This second point encouraged us, because without Croatian legislation being in force, no decisions of the Croatian government could be implemented in the Krajina, which meant there would be no persecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how did the Croatian authorities that you mentioned look on the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise in advance for possibly insulting the UN and the Security Council. In its documents, which later became the documents of the Security Council, the Croatian side always used the term "the so-called Vance Plan," and the UN never reacted to this, although the Serb side kept drawing attention to it. On the other hand, these documents were distributed bearing a Security Council number. Furthermore, our warnings that this important document of the Security Council was being disparaged were not distributed in the United Nations palace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the most important document on which the situation in the UN protected areas was based at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The only document was the Vance Plan. All the other documents we hoped would only be used to implement that plan. However, if I'm not wrong, starting from Resolution 815 onwards, the UN protected area was already being treated as a province or area of the Republic of Croatia. Sovereignty was being transferred to the UN protected area, although the Vance Plan stated that there would be no such prejudging of the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how did the international community treat the Vance-Owen --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Vance Plan, interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- adopted by the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The international community was neglectful. It didn't defend the Vance Plan. The international community, through the documents of the Security Council, wrote that the Republika Srpska Krajina, or the UN protected area, was an integral part of the Republic of Croatia. This amounted to prejudging the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How was the issue of weapons resolved on the territory of the Republika Srpska Krajina in the UN protected areas?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The Vance Plan provided for heavy weapons to be put under a double key. One key was in the keeping of the Serbian army of the Krajina, and the other key was in the keeping of UNPROFOR officers. The police of the Republika Srpska Krajina was also supposed to be disarmed and to carry only sidearms. This means pistols without long barrels. This provision was the only one that could not be implemented by the government of the Republika Srpska Krajina, because every day the Croats perpetrated aggression against the territory of the Republika Srpska Krajina, and in the case of large-scale aggression such as that which occurred at Miljevac plateau or Ravni Kotor on the 22nd of January, 1993, and then on the 8th of September, 1993. At such times UNPROFOR officers were always aware of the tragedy that might happen to the Serbian people, and they themselves offered the army of Republika Srpska Krajina the keys to the weapons depots so that they could take the weapons and fight off the army of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When the Vance Plan was adopted, did the citizens of the leadership of the Republika Srpska Krajina expect to be protected by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, they did expect that, although many had doubts. Many had doubts precisely because the international media were so anxious to show that the Croats were in the wrong and the Croats --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That the Serbs, interpreter's correction, were in the wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the Croats were in the right. The editorial policy of the media was to ignore and be silent about the mass expulsions of Serbs from the Croatian territories. Had this not been so, there would have been greater confidence in the United Nations on the part of the Serbs. But I think that for the first time now this terrible fact, which is 15 years old, will reach the headlines of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the UN protected areas, which was their official title, did UNPROFOR provide protection to the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, they did not provide any protection at all. You know, as does probably the Chamber, that in every Croatian offensive UN soldiers got killed. It's quite possible that more than was acknowledged were actually killed, and it's quite surprising that in such a situation the Security Council did not threaten Croatia with sanctions, to say the least, or with war planes, as they later did against Serbia and Montenegro in a situation which was less terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These facts and the attacks that took place after the adoption of the Vance Plan and the expectations that the Serbs in those areas would be protected, how did all this affect the situation on the UN protected areas and the population there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the people were disappointed, Mr. President, and the government realised that what was most important to people was to save their families. After the Miljevac plateau and Ravni Kotari, the population of the Krajina started dispersing. Suddenly they started moving away to Serbia, the Republika Srpska, and Montenegro. However, this was not really dramatic, and in early 1993, as the minister of foreign affairs, I drew the attention of the government and the president to the fact that the population of the Krajina and Bosnia and Herzegovina, who were Serbs, would start moving away to foreign countries. We predicted that visas would be given wholesale to people from the Serbian Krajina to foreign countries, and this actually happened. The United Nations even opened up an office in Belgrade where it was very easy to obtain visas very fast to emigrate to Australia, Canada, America, the European countries, Sweden and Norway. The people felt that they could not believe that the UN military forces would protect them, and they began to look for ways of saving themselves and their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As of mid-1992, when the UN forces took over control over the whole area, apart from these large-scale attacks you've already mentioned, the Miljevac plateau, Maslenica, the Medak pocket, and so on, was there any other fighting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Croatia did not behave honourably towards the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina either. I cannot give you the exact date in 1991 when Croatian troops crossed the Sava and attacked the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is an area called Posavina. However, UN documents - and this is ridiculous - said it was elements of the Croatian army that had crossed the Sava. An aggression against a state should be defined quite differently. Sometime in 1991, Croatia threatened the eastern part of the Republika Srpska Krajina. I don't know the exact number of civilians whom they called in a field while they were gathering maize were killed. They killed a group and took another group prisoner. Fortunately, at the request of UNPROFOR, these people were returned safe and sound to the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the government of the Republika Srpska Krajina submit any documents about the crimes against the Serbs in the Republika Srpska Krajina after the peace forces of the UN arrived?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the office of the Ministry of the Foreign Affairs there was a man working practically around the clock, who speaks English really well, and he translated everything and sent it out to foreign countries in Europe, to the Security Council, and to the Secretary-General. However, none of these documents was ever accorded the status of an official document in any UN body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in what form did the authorities of the Republic of Srpska Krajina react or did they react? Did they go to the UN because of the violation of the peace agreement and attacks on the UNPA zones and attacks on the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I've already said everything was -- there was just silence. That's where everything stopped. There was silence, and the world media, mass media, did not inform about the situation in the way that they should have sent out information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. At that time, apart from sending what you did to the United Nations, you also communicated with Marrack Goulding, did you not, who at the time was in your office very frequently, came to see you frequently on behalf of UNPROFOR. Do you have any data about that communication?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I never met Marrack Goulding myself because his activities took place in 1991 and 1992 before my arrival, but I do know - I learnt about this later on - that he did intervene at a point in time, I believe, when the Croatian government or, rather, the president, Tudjman, when he announced that he would not be accepting the Vance Plan. That's when he intervened, and I think that was on the 2nd of January, 1992, when that letter of Tudjman's to the UN came that it accepted the Vance Plan. So his activities were in that regard, and as I say, I was not in Knin myself at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, after the attack on the Maslenica bridge, did the Serb representatives continue to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Serb representatives always attended negotiations, regardless of where the initiative came from. For example, when the initiative came from the Croatian government for negotiations, through Vollebaek who testified here, we accepted that too. We didn't consult you or Belgrade, as the Prosecution and their witnesses are prone to state and accuse you of doing, we accepted it straight away. And that's a rather interesting event. Vollebaek, on the 8th of September, 1993, in Knin, brought a draft agreement of the Croatian government which we were supposed to sign. And while he was opening his file, the dossier on that, the Croatian army attacked the Medak pocket, and as French General Cot said, it burnt everything down, and not even cats and dogs survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to the agreement that was brought by Vollebaek?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he closed his file on that, went back to Zagreb, and did not utter a word of condemnation of the Croats. Had I been duped like that by somebody, I would have at least left my post, left my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about the negotiations in Geneva between March and June. What happened in the negotiations in Erdut? What happened there? Who took part? What happened? What were the contents of those negotiations? Who negotiated? What was the subject of the negotiations, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the talks in Geneva were unsuccessful, just as the ones in Washington had been, and that is why the international mediators undertook something that they thought would lead to fruit, would bear fruit. Let me tell you about Geneva. I put my initials to an agreement put forward by Lord Owen, but I was not authorised myself nor was the president of the state, Hadzic, authorised to sign it because Krajina, pursuant to that agreement, would be included into Croatia without any guarantees or without the creation of a two-nation Croatian state. So we said that we would present it to the Assembly, and if the Assembly, as the supreme legislative organ, adopts it, then it would come into force. However, the Assembly rejected it unanimously and that is why the international mediators invited us to come to Erdut on the 15th of July, 1993. They came, Charles Redman came, the deputy foreign minister of the United States, and Vitaliy Churkin, the deputy foreign minister of the Russian Federation, two of the most powerful countries. And they said that we should sign the agreement so that finally there would be an end to the bloodshed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was that? That was in 1993, you say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. May I just be allowed to continue and tell you this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: They thought - and that's what they did - they proposed the draft for the agreement. It did not contain many points, but it did provide for commissions to be set up for all forms of state activity. And they told us in confidence that the agreement could lead to cooperation in all spheres of life and a two-nation state of the kind that existed in 1990. Now, I signed that particular agreement, and the sole condition that we posed of the Croats was that it shouldn't be signed by some police official or somebody from Franjo Tudjman's security force but somebody at the level of the person signing for Krajina. And the Croats agreed to that proviso, and it was signed by the minister of trade. I'm afraid I can't remember his name, first or last name, just now, but the most important point of the negotiations was the following: Richard or, rather, Redman -- Charles Redman, that's right. Charles Redman said: "Gentlemen of the Krajina, this agreement must be respected by the Croats and must be put into effect. The guarantor for that is the Russian Federation. Mr. Churkin will be in charge of intervening if the Croats happen to reject this agreement as well."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened next? Perhaps I interrupted you, but tell us what happened next with that agreement.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were satisfied to hear that, especially as Churkin said "Gentlemen, if that happens, if Croatia does that, then I will arrive in Knin and then travel to Zagreb, and we will put this agenda up again and put it into practice." And a copy of that agreement can be found in the UN Security Council, because in a report by the UN Secretary-General, it said that this had to do with the well-being of the people and that it will be -- put an end to the bloodshed along the border between Srpska Krajina and Croatia. And Boutros-Ghali said some very nice things about the agreement in his report. However, not much time went by when Franjo Tudjman -- I don't know what -- on what occasion, said that that was one of 40 agreements, in fact, which Croatia had signed but had not abided by and that it would not abide by the present one either. And so pursuant to counselling from Charles Redman, we sent a fax to Mr. Churkin and asked him to come to Knin himself, because that was the guarantee provided by the two superpowers. There was no point in a small country like Croatia in the Balkans playing with the guarantees issued by these two major powers. And Churkin didn't answer. I sent him a telegram saying that I would come to Moscow, and I set off the following day. However, when I arrived, the ministry of the Russian Federation, the Russian Foreign Ministry, told me that Churkin had left for Brussels on an official visit, and I was received by Potoni [phoen], the foreign minister, Ivanov, and he said he didn't wish to discuss the matter, discuss the agreement at all. That was a surprise. That came as a surprise. We didn't expect to hear that, because everybody thought that Russia was a friend unreservedly of the Serbs. But he said he didn't want to talk to him. And I asked him, "Well, why did I come to Moscow, then?" And he said, "So that you Serbs could learn to live together with the Muslims and Croats just like we live together with the Chechens and other Muslims." So that was all he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what actually happened in Croatia after the signing of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what happened? Nothing happened. The international mediators were left without a document guaranteeing what had been stipulated by the Vance Plan, that is to say to find a peaceful solution between the two ethnic communities. And of course the international mediators did not apologise. They came to Knin, demanding that we negotiate again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So did they say, forget the Erdut agreement, you have to negotiate again?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Or did they say you would be negotiating on the basis of the Erdut agreement and the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm mixing my words now, words that sound similar. But anyway, they said forget the agreement, although it was signed at a high level, if you look at the Croatian side, because for our part we always -- it was always government members that signed it. But anyway, they proposed that we conduct secret negotiations so that we should not lose face. And we agreed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Was that after Vollebaek's visit to Knin?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, after, because the September -- the 9th of September one fell through, as I've explained. The 9th of September was after the Erdut agreement. So after the Erdut agreement, Vollebaek -- there was Vollebaek in Knin. Now, Vollebaek proposed secret negotiations in Norway this time, if you're interested in hearing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, did you go to attend those secret negotiations in Norway?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
