utterances.text: Yes, we did. The head of the delegation was President Hadzic, and in the delegation next to him was the justice minister, Kuzet, and I myself as the foreign minister. And I think there was another man, and that was Admiral Rakic. We had an interpreter, and I assume that the Trial Chamber will be interested in this. His name was Boro Bozic, not the man who testified here, Lazarevic. He was just a private interpreter for President Hadzic who helped him tour the cultural monuments in places where we went to, to help him with trade, but that was official because the head of state, whatever he does he does officially. So we negotiated and the head of the Croatian delegation was Hrvoje Sarinic, and I think that at the time he was an advisor to President Tudjman and the head of state security, I believe. Unless I'm much mistaken. He was a Croat who lived in South America for a long time -- no, in South Africa it was, and who had happened to come back to Croatia quite recently, but he wasn't an extremist and I have nothing bad to say about the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So tell us what happened during the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: During the negotiations, the delegation of the Republika Srpska Krajina was highly cooperative. The draft agreement which Vollebaek put before us, to us and the Croatian delegation, we for our part accepted, and it was aimed at achieving something similar to what would have been achieved by the Erdut agreement which Croatia rejected. Then, Mr. President, we didn't mind losing out on the Erdut agreement too much, because we thought, well, here we have a new agreement, almost identical. We'll sign that. And it was supposed to have been signed in the morning of that day. In the morning, Vollebaek called all the journalists from Oslo to attend. We were 60 kilometres outside Oslo - I forget the name of the place now - and we were happy. We just asked a room, some premises in which we could prepare the material, and then to inform the following day our public at home and the world public, and there was really no difference, not on any of the points between the agreement -- or between us and the Croats. There was general harmony. And we even joked about it. We played a little chess amongst ourselves. I was a better chess player, so I was able to beat the interpreter, too, although he is master level, master candidate category, but that was the general mood that prevailed. And when we went into that room to prepare our report for the next day, our liaison officer that very evening, it might have been 11.00, perhaps midnight, gave us a message from Zagreb saying that Tudjman had ordered his delegation to pack up and go home early the next morning and that they were not allowed to sign the agreement which Tudjman had a copy of on his table, on his own desk. And this is -- it's only us that knew that. But Vollebaek didn't know about that. We knew about it, the Croats knew about it, but Vollebaek didn't, so we wanted to take advantage of informing our centre in Knin and Belgrade during the night that Tudjman had vetoed the signing of the agreement which should have been the crowning of the negotiations in Norway. The next day the journalists turned up, they knew about Tudjman's decision. The only person who didn't know about his decision was Vollebaek, who had organised and conducted the negotiations. And he was very angry with me. He said: "You've ruined my career. Why did you inform the public beforehand about all that?" And that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. May I just remind you to give shorter answers. That answer took up the entire page on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it was interesting, unless I'm very much mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you say so yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So those negotiations, the secret negotiations in Norway fell through, did they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because Tudjman sent a letter once you had dovetailed everything and harmonised everything, saying that you weren't to sign.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were supposed to sign in front of the Norwegian journalists, those who were accredited in Oslo, and they were informed to arrive that night. But on their way there, they had already learnt that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, so the negotiations fell through. Now, did you continue negotiating?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, the international mediators asked us once again to negotiate, without criticising Croatia. They didn't even write it down in a single document. And Dobanovci was the chosen venue, which is the holiday home of the former president, Josip Broz Tito, some 20 kilometres away from Belgrade, and that's where we met. Once again the Croatian delegation was led by Hrvoje Sarinic, and the Republic of Srpska Krajina was headed by Goran Hadzic, its president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that successful?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. It was even more ludicrous, if I can put it that way, because Sarinic interrupted the negotiations, and he had harmonised the text, which resembled the Norwegian one and the one from Erdut, but when it came to the question of separation, a separation line and regarding the 22nd of January Croatian aggression, they stated that it was state property and the state had nationalised the fields and orchards which belonged to Serb proprietors. Now, a man named Kuzet, the justice minister who was born in those regions, said, "Mr. Sarinic, you can't have this plantation belong to Croatia when each bit of land is owned by Serb farmers." Mr. Sarinic used this. He jumped up and said, "The president did not authorise me to hand over this plantation." He got his things together and stormed out of the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can't say that negotiations fell through because of that plantation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So those negotiations fell through as well. What happened afterwards? Was another round of negotiations scheduled later on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And now we thought they had to succeed because Charles Redman turned up again and Vitaliy Churkin. On the 22nd of March and we were supposed to negotiate in Croatia in Zagreb. Up until that time, we never agreed to go and negotiate on Croatian territory because the Croats interpreted this as the rebel Serbs arriving to attend negotiations with their state organs. However, everything fell through again, but on that occasion we agreed and we said, right, we're not going to go into that formality and make any problems. We agreed. We said, right, the negotiations will take place at the Russian embassy. That's what Churkin and Redman had decided. We didn't ask for any protective measures or anything like that. We would have gone to any presidential palace or whatever to attend negotiations. And those negotiations were fairly successful. The text of the negotiations was excellent for one fact, because of one basic fact: Heavy weaponry on the part of the Croatia should have been placed under control as well as heavy weapons of the Republic of Srpska Krajina. It was to be placed under control. And this was the first time that we were present as equal partners, at least where it came to weapons, and we signed the agreement on the 29th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was the agreement put into practice? Was it implemented?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Never. We always asked the international mediators, UNPROFOR officers, why they shouldn't effect control over Croatian weapons and arming, and if our heavy weapons were placed at precisely the spot distant from the border where it was supposed to be placed, why wasn't Croatian weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you because you've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you sit down to a new round of negotiations after that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me just think about this. I have to remember all the sequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about any negotiations scheduled for London, for instance, between Krajina and Croatia, organised by the Foreign Ministry of Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was done in agreement with the Foreign Ministry of Britain and the Congress of Serbian Unification. Let me tell you, that's a Serb organisation in the United States of America, with branch offices in Europe too. And also there was a humanitarian organisation, a British one. I had all the documents about that, but the only thing that attracted us to those negotiations was a message we received from the Foreign Ministry of the United Kingdom saying that the Croatian delegation would also be coming to the negotiations. I didn't consult Belgrade, although I lived in Belgrade, or with any organ in Serbia, didn't consult with you. Since I was the person informed about the negotiations as the former foreign minister, they contacted me, that is to say London did, and I sent a fax to Knin, and I was going to go there myself to expound why it would be useful to go to London at a government meeting, because Great Britain would be the auspices. It would be held under their patronage because we didn't -- and that although we didn't succeed with the patronage of the USA and Russia, we thought we might succeed this time. But President Martic and Prime Minister Mikelic gave the go-ahead for the negotiations and told me to go alone, without taking any other member with me. And that really did succeed. It was secret until even the present day. Nobody knew about these negotiations scheduled to take place on 60 miles out of London. I was told that it was in one of Cromwell's 60th century castles, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's leave out the historical details. Tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I waited for five days and the Croats never turned up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone? Did you talk to anyone about anything?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I was only received in the foreign office of Great Britain. They wanted to hear my views. They reprimanded me there. They said that we Serbs were people who looked into the past and that we were supposed to look into the future. At that meeting I said the following -- now, this was the head of the department for the Eastern Adriatic. I think that his name was Mr. Rion [phoen]. He said that -- he was Irish, too, and he said, "See how we and the English get along. You see the post that I have here now." And then I said to him, "In any pub in Great Britain you can hear people talking about what happened in Ireland in terms of the history of Great Britain, so why can we not speak about being part of Austro-Hungary?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You've been through all the negotiations that you took part in now. If you omitted some, let's not dwell on it any longer anyway. Several times it was mentioned here, and also in some of the witness statements coming from the other side, that I gave you instructions before the negotiations that you had. I see that you had many negotiations. Please answer the following question: Did I give you instructions, or any of my co-workers, in terms of how you would negotiate on behalf of the Republic of Serb Krajina with the representatives of Croatia or the representatives of the international community?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am confident that you did not even know about my trip to London.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about London now. After all, the trip to London is not the most important one of all. You talked about negotiations in New York, in Geneva, in Norway. I don't know if you mentioned any other talks, but all of those that you mentioned, did I give you any instructions in terms of these negotiations of yours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Never. No instructions whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of a simple answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I did not give you any instructions in terms of these negotiations, could I have given instructions to anyone else without you knowing about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, my bosses, and then they could have conveyed it to me. But then I was the one who wrote out all those texts on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so you prepared the documents for these negotiations, the platforms?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to give a brief answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did your bosses exercise any influence over your making of these preparatory documents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It's interesting that they never raised any objections. What I have to point out is our trip to Washington. In the platform, the document for those meetings, I did not say that we would immediately let the Croats use the road, the airport, and the power plant, but Mr. Hadzic, although this had not been in my platform, proposed that first of all as the first concession to be given by the Republic of Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you talk about Washington, that's a separate set of negotiations from New York, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm so sorry. It was New York, and I misspoke. I said Washington. I am so sorry. It happens to elderly people, what can I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about political parties in Krajina. You said that there were several of them, and you said that you were not the member of any party.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you followed the activity of all parties, I assume?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as much as I could, because you see that I kept travelling abroad. I was abroad pretty often. And then when I would come back - perhaps the Trial Chamber is not interested in that - but we had about 70 representative offices of volunteers abroad, and I had to communicate with all of them, so I'm not that aware of the life of political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether anybody from Serbia influenced the establishment of these political parties?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I don't know how useful my testimony's going to be, but I can note the following: The people who founded the Serb Democratic Party for the most part were your political opponents. For example, until his death, that is what Dr. Raskovic was. And Dr. Milan Babic then. If that's what you were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Milan Babic hasn't died yet.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he's alive. I didn't say anything different from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Out of all the members of the leadership of the Serb Krajina, perhaps you were the person who communicated the most or, rather, who spent the largest amount of time -- time in Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it was at my proposal that the government accepted that the Ministry of the Interior --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the Foreign Ministry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- should be in Belgrade, because there was a wide array of embassies and consulates from all the over the world there. We spoke to many ambassadors on their people, asking them to open offices in Krajina, but that was out of the question. So that was the only solution that we could work out for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, in view of your experience and in view of problems of the Serb people in Krajina, in the indictment, in the part that speaks about responsibility in 26(m), it says I controlled, contributed or otherwise utilised Serb state-run media outlets to manipulate Serbian public opinion by spreading exaggerated and false messages of ethnically based attacks by Croats against Serb people in order to create an atmosphere of fear and hatred among Serbs living in Serbia and Croatia. The propaganda generated by the Serbian media was an important tool in contributing to the perpetration of crimes in Croatia. Please, in view of your experience, in view of your presence there, can you say whether this is true, whether all of this that is claimed here is true or --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, had that been so, then the media - I mean if you had control over them - would first and foremost write about the expulsion of Serbs from Croatian towns and cities, and that was not mentioned by the media in Serbia, especially not by radio and television there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was your experience? Did the media in Serbia exaggerate false messages about ethnically based attacks against Serbs, and did they fan hatred?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, they only diminished the proportions of all of this. Things that were going on were in actual fact far worse than that was portrayed in the Serb media. For example, on the 1st of May, 1995, the attack in Slavonia. The main news programme of TV Belgrade carried that particular bit of news only in the 17th minute of their programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was there a fanning of hatred against Croats in the Serb media?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Never. No Serb ever uttered things like what Tanja Torbarina wrote. Or if you compare it to what the Muslim and the Croat media said, Seselj, who is accused here of disseminating hatred, he was almost a saint. I cannot even utter the words that were written and said there. They are worse than any kind of swear word you could imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Milan Babic. He testified here. In his testimony on the 18th of November, 2002, and that is on transcript page 12947, 82, 84, I'm not going to quote everything he said, but he said that I spread hatred between the Serbs and the Croats, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, that statement is totally nonsensical if it has to do with your character. You did not go against your own political enemies in Serbia, let alone somebody outside Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Babic also stated that: "It is strange that Spegelj was accused of buying weapons from Hungary, and that videotape that was shown by the federal Ministry for National Defence, because Milosevic said that he personally bought weapons from Hungary." Can you interpret this statement? It was on transcript page 13104 and 106.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand you, Mr. President, especially the latter part of your sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he challenged the whole story about Spegelj. And we saw what the Hungarian minister had to say to our minister. He challenged all that. He disputed all that. He will that I bought weapons from Hungary. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please observe the pause between question and answer. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Mr. Milosevic is misquoting the witness Babic. Of course we have to check first, but I remember very closely that he actually said that he saw the Spegelj tape and that he was shocked about what Spegelj was doing and those kind of things. I remember that very vividly. So I think that's not right, what he's quoted here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you're quoting the transcript, then you must be accurate. Are you in a position to substantiate?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assumed that I was correct, but he stated on transcript page 13550 to 552. And now this is even spelling it out in more precise terms than what I put in my question. "Every time when the officials of the Republic of Serb Krajina met with the Croats or foreign negotiators, they had to consult with Milosevic in order to get instructions. If somebody would oppose that, they would be dismissed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were the one who conducted the negotiations. How did this work? Is what Babic says here correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It's not correct, and I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Babic, in relation to the JNA - and that is on transcript page 13270 to 74, 75 - he says that: "In August 1991, the JNA stopped protecting only the Serbs in Krajina and, together with other units under its command, they took part in the destruction of non-Serb populations, setting up new boundaries that went beyond the boundaries established through the Krajina referendum." On the basis of your own knowledge, can you assess this? Can you assess the behaviour of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I think that this is pure nonsense. He said that they stopped protecting the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They stopped protecting the Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so they -- protecting them until then. That is to say that they had been in danger. So I can understand that, then, but the Yugoslav People's Army never took part in any persecutions of the non-Serb population. And after all, until the end of 1991, the Yugoslav People's Army was not a Serb army or the Serb army at the time of the fighting at Vukovar, for instance. The commander of the air force was a Croat, Zvonko Jurjevic. I think that Babic here is equating this JNA from 1991 to a purely Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This witness also says that -- or, rather, do you know these names: Boro Rasuo and Risto Matkovic. He mentions them as people who worked with me, and he said at that time they worked on drafts for the SAO Krajina. Do you know anything about that? Irrespective of this these particular people, but can you say anything about this? Were laws for Krajina written in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I never met Matkovic. I have met Boro Rasuo. He joined the government when I ceased being foreign minister. I heard that Rasuo took part in writing the legislation of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, and it is certain that they looked at the legislation of Croatia and at the legislation of Serbia when writing the laws of the Republic of Serb Krajina. There is nothing dishonourable about that. People write laws the way they do in any country, Krajina included.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information about this that someone from Belgrade, for example -- well, if these laws were not written in Belgrade, did anybody from Belgrade suggest to them how they should write some laws? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: My deputy, Petkovic, Srecko Petkovic, deputy foreign minister, I know that he personally took part in the writing of these laws and that he did that in Knin. He probably consulted, say, the laws of Russia or Croatia, and perhaps even Roman law, of course. He took part in the writing of these legal documents. I don't know about other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Babic claims that Territorial Defence commanders reported directly to the Yugoslav People's Army and not to the government of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The transcript page is 12983. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, one should know what the Territorial Defence is. The Territorial Defence was envisaged by the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Municipalities were in charge of Territorial Defence. Secretariats for National Defence within the municipalities. And that is how they were established. However, they respected the command of the then-JNA. As the JNA disappeared from Slovenia or Croatia and Krajina, new armies were born and new Territorial Defences were born. As for Krajina, one should bear in mind the following: In some municipalities there were no secretariats that could have been inherited, so to speak, but some people who had fled from Croatian towns, they did what they could and, together with the people they found there, they comprised the Territorial Defence. How could every Territorial Defence unit report to Belgrade? That is quite unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He added on that same transcript page that Milosevic directly appointed Territorial Defence commanders in Krajina through the existence of the government of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: This is an incomprehensible assertion. The authority of the Krajina government did not differ from the authority exercised by any government in the world. It is true that our government maintained relations with the governments of other countries as much as possible. We did have relations with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but always as any other two countries would. And of course that we can consult each other, help each other, exchange experts. Just one more thing, with your permission: I think that we should not understand things to mean that at one point in time the Yugoslav federal state died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is your answer to the question that Mr. Milosevic asked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have answered. They were not consulted. We decided on our own at government sessions. We made decisions about everything, even including trade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you would have been in a position to know if Mr. Milosevic had directly appointed Territorial Defence commanders in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That kind of question was never raised at government meetings, but the General Staff reported to us about the appointments of officers, commanders, and so on. We never even asked about how they became candidates, on what conditions, and how they were appointed; whether it was one general who decided, two generals, the entire General Staff, et cetera. I don't know about that, because everybody was in charge of their own affairs. The government was informed about what I did in the ministry, and the General Staff informed about what was going on in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Babic claims, on page 12997 all the way to 13427, 668, 691, that through parallel structures Milosevic provoked incidents that then in turn led to a reaction of fear among the Serb population and intensified reactions of the Croatian police, and this led to intolerance, violence, all the way up to war. I presented very briefly what he had asserted. What can you say about that, Mr. Jarcevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: That is sheer nonsense. The situation was quite different from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The last question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Babic said that at the end of 1990, tension escalated and that a group headed by Milan Martic, president of the National Council that was dealing with repression against the Serbs, and all of this was done in the hope that the mounting of tensions in parts of Croatia could allow the Yugoslav authorities to interfere, to introduce a state of emergency, and to suspend the authority of the Croatian authorities. That is what he said on the 19th of November, 2002, on transcript page 14104, 105, and 119. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: This is sheer nonsense yet again, squared. We saw how things happened and what happened in Croatian towns. How could Milan Martic or anybody else influence what was going on there? The plan of the Croatian state was the extermination of the Serbs or the persecution or expulsion of the Serbs. There is nothing else I can say but that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I was told that tab -- the Resolution 762 was not admitted. What you referred to is Resolution 752.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I misread 752 for 762.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that being the case, we have to admit tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, my reference was to 752.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we will admit tab 12. I thank Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, take a look at this. In this binder of exhibits, you have a few Resolutions, and it says translation for -- provided for each and every one of them. So these are Resolutions 740, 743, 802, 815, that have to do with the evidence of Mr. Jarcevic in view of the office he held. I thought that there was no reason for me to make copies of Security Council Resolutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Those are the exhibits which were already admitted, but this one was not admitted. And for the sake of completeness, I would admit tab 18, but let's consider that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We are adjourned.
